reviewText: I've been a Tori Amos "ears with feet" since I first heard Little Earthquakes so many years ago. When I first heard about this project, I wondered how Tori could ever select 20 songs to represent her Atlantic records career. I think she did an amazing job, though of course there are some omissions, the main one being "Caught a Lite Sneeze" from Boys for Pele. I also wish she could have included something from the Y Kant Tori Read era, perhaps a studio version of the reworked "Cool on Your Island" that she did on the Scarlet's Walk tour.That said, the songs here are chosen with care, and all are remixed/reworked, with four new recordings (two brand new songs and two re-recorded B sides).Tori has never sounded crisper. The reworked tracks from Little Earthquakes especially stand out. The original recording sounded a bit muddy, but now these songs sound crystal clear and make me wish the entire Little Earthquakes disc could be remastered. The only real "miss" in the disc is the inclusion of the dance remix of Professional Widow vs. the album version.The bonus DVD is also a nice addition, it includes 2 Dolby 5.1 remixes, 3 live recordings from soundtracks, and 2 instrumental versions of songs (over the menus). I wish the DVD contained more materil, but then that probably would have boosted the price of the collection so I understand why this compromise was made.

reviewText: I only started listening to Hip-Hop seriously a few years ago, and this was the first Nas album i'd ever heard.  I picked it up after hearing I Can on the radio, I loved this track though soon realised it was nowhere near the best song on the album.  Gods Son is a great album, it made me want to buy all of Nas' other albums.Notable tracks include the Eminem produced The Cross, Get Down, Book of Rhymes, Made You Look and Warrior Song and also Thugz Mansion N.Y (is Tupac turning in his grave?).  If I were reccomending 1 Nas album it would be Illmatic and if you like that then this is an essential purchase.  Nas goes deeper in Gods Son than probably any of his other material, mainly because of the recent death of his mother, and no track highlights this more than Dance, a heartfelt tribute to Ann Jones.I have re-written this review as I originally gave it 4 stars, but on listening more it deserves a 5.  The only bad track is Zone Out (which is possibly Nas' worst track ever), but every other song is great, I would put Gods Son on a par with Stillmatic as his second best album.

reviewText: I don't think that Fiona Apple's sophmore release is bad, I just think that it pales in comparison to Tidal. And while this is less than extradinary, it is, however, much better than some other similar disappiontments in recent years, such as Strange Little Girls by Tori Amos and Exciter by Depeche Mode. The lyrics (though not as good as Tidal's) are as witty as ever, but while the dark sarcasm is still evident it's not as forward as on Tidal. I also find the songs to have weaker melody lines that are thin on hooking the listener. The piano parts are also less beautiful here with more chaotic chords that seem to go nowhere. The only songs that really strike me as being good are "The Way Things Are" and her first single, "Fast As You Can". I just love how she sings really quick on the verses and then slows things down on the soothing bridge release only to pick things up again in a feverish tornado. I even tried singing it once but found myself laughing too much because I didn't know the words very well... (LOL!). I just hope that when and if she does bring another album out that it will be better than this less than stellar follow-up to a grammy-worthy debut.P.S. - If you understand what the title means in full than please oblige me by letting me know!

reviewText: For those of you who consider yourselves avid music listeners, just look at the tracklisting of Mariah Carey's Greatest Hits album, and you'll know that this 2-disc album is necessary for your collection.  You'll think to yourself, "My, she has had a great career and released a lot of songs!"  When comparing this album to her "# 1's" album, naturally, this one of more complete because, although all of this music didn't reach the top of the charts, it's still the best of Mariah.  This album contains basically everything that Mariah and her camp has ever released to radio, and the finished product is memorable because, regardless your age, there is at least one Mariah song that will recollect some personal, fond memories.  That five octave vocal range is, of course, here, but mostly on the first couple of songs.  This album includes every tempo of music: uptempo songs, midtempo music and, Mariah's strength, the ballads.  With ballads, Mariah is able to really allow her listeners to hear the greatness of her voice (although sometimes she strains her voice because she hits notes incorrectly on occasion.)  In total, there are 28 songs here, so some of the material is better than others.  Honestly, her early material is much better than the music released more recently, but it's all worth listening to.One of Mariah's strongest songs lyrically is the first song she ever released, "Vision of Love."  When I was younger, I was not a fan of this song, but as I grew more mature and actually took the time to listen to the lyrics, I enjoy and appreciate this song; it is undoubtedly one of her best.  Her best uptempo song?  Come on now, that has to go to "Dreamlover."  That song makes you want to get up and dance, sing along, and just recall great junctures in your life.  The production is out of this world!  Mariah's most successful song is "One Sweet Day", which features male quartet Boyz II Men.  This is another track I didn't care for until I was older and took a listen to the lyrics.  This song is about the hope of seeing deceased loved ones again.  In my opinion, it's still not her best song, but great nonetheless.  "Hero" is arguably Mariah's signature song, and there's no need to wonder why.  This song was played or performed at countless graduations and other ceremonies because the message is so important: There is no need to look up to other people, because you are a natural hero, a natural role model.  Mariah isn't afraid to let the world know that she believes in God.  Just take a listen to "Thank God I Found You", "When You Believe", and a song dedicated solely to Him, "Make It Happen."  That vocal range is very present in "Make It Happen." Speaking of which, if one really is really interested in her vocal range, "Emotions" is the song for them to listen to.  Mariah has never showcased her vocal range like she did at the end of that song!  It's one of my personal Mariah favorites.You need this masterpiece in your collection, there is no arguing that fact.  Mariah has sold over 100 million records and is one of the most successful female artists ever.  This greatest hits album enlightens us as to why she has been such a huge success.  She's immensely talented!Mikeisha's Top 5 (Boy, it's difficult picking out just 5)1. "Dreamlover"2. "Love Takes Time"3. "Hero"4. "Emotions"5. "Always Be My Baby"

reviewText: It took John Hiatt awhile to find his voice as a songwriter and his style as a performer. His early efforts hinted at the later, greater things in store for this talented troubadour. Tiki Bar is another in a string of strong albums from this gifted man. The album's nearest relative is (not surprisingly) Slow Turning in terms of its sound. The Goners make a welcome return and clearly have helped to revitalize Hiatt's muse. The album before this was such a stylistic detour that it really can't be compared to his latest work. The risk of repeating without deepening or changing the sound on his latest album was certainly there and Hiatt manages to leap this hurtle at full speed and land perfectly.Every song is a gem and very little is miscalculated. The production by Jay Joyce is the most sympathetic Hiatt has had since he worked with Glyn Johns over a decade ago. It's also one of the most rewarding partnerships in Hiatt's career. The only other album that manages to demonstrate the songwriting power and stylistic sweep of Tiki is Hiatt's trio of classics from the late 80's and his mid-90's classic Walk On.Hiatt is one of America's greatest underappreciated talent. From the rollicking opening bars of Everybody Went Low to stylistic and funky closer Father Stars, Hiatt manages to touch on the musical approaches that have worked for him in the past. These two tracks map the musical extremes on this great album; Hiatt's backing band manage to fill the songs with color that helps to make the songs more appealing without sacrificing Hiatt's unique world view.He also manages to deepen and expand on his musical vocabulary. At this stage in his career I wouldn't expect that to occur. Most artist's end up repeating themselves with mixed success. Hiatt has continued to hone his songwriting skills. He's also continued to grow as a vocalist as well. His expressive voice still has that powerful, bluesy growl but there's a tenderness lurking beneath only hinted at before.Listening to The Tiki Bar Is Open reminds me of reading a rich, powerful novel; everytime I come back to it I discover something new.

reviewText: After the celebrated, but uneven and very angry "Jagged Little Pill", Alanis Morrissette in 1998 released her most diverse and, put simply, best record yet. On "Junkie", teaming again with producer Glen Ballard, Alanis is more mature and less militant than on "Pill", sophisticatedly improving her songwriting qualities, while providing more glimpses to her complicated personality.Generous in offering 17 songs, some of this rock album's are outright gems ("Unsent", "Joining You"), some show really eclectic taste ("Thank You", "So Pure"). Failures can also be found, mainly "Sympathetic Character" with its meaningful message but, alas, with completely inadequate musical side. Guitars are dominating, often with impressive results ("Baba", "Can't Not", "Would Not Come"). Morissette's traditionally overlapping lyrics sometimes work out right ("The Couch"), sometimes not ("Your Congratulations"). "One" and "UR" are plain good songs, as is "That I Would Be Good", which seems to be tapping from the roots of Alanis' great compatriot Sarah McLachlan.Sophomore efforts seldom exceed the quality of debuts ("Jagged Little Pill" is usually considered Morissette's real debut). "Junkie" did, although the sales did not indicate that. The problem was that "Junkie" lacked the hype of "Pill", enhanced by the handful of Grammies. That's usual music irony.

reviewText: Though "On Fire" may be an awesome song, it's not enough to warrant buying "The Hunger For More". Most of the tracks aren't too good, but a few good songs are scattered here and there. Unfortunately, Lloyd Banks isn't a very charismatic or fun rapper (he's a tad better than 50 Cent, though) which definitely doesn't help the songs. The production is pretty good at times, however (most notably on "On Fire" and "Warrior Part 2"). Compared to Young Buck's or 50 Cent's album, though, the production here is much worse. Once again, G-Unit raps about how cool they are which is REALLY getting old (why can't rappers be inspired by all the great oldschool rap albums out there?). Overall this isn't a terrible album - it's just "decent". You'd be much happier with "Get Rich Or Die Tryin'" and (possibly) "Straight Outta Ca$hville". ONLY for mainstream rap fans (although "On Fire" might be appealing to others).Highlights include:"Ain't No Click""Playboy" (sort of)"Warrior""On Fire""I Get High""I'm So Fly" (sort of)"Work Magic" (the beat is at least good...)"Warrior Part 2""Til The End"
summary: Definitely not as good as Young Buck's or 50 Cent's album, but it's decent - 3.5 stars

reviewText: Like other reviewers, I bought this mainly for "Crazy".  I also agree that this album is not for everyone.  Don't expect every song to be fun and bouncy - "Just a Thought" is about suicide, and "Necromancing" is about necrophilia.  I think that these songs don't really fit in with the rest of the album, and that's why I give St. Elsewhere four stars.  Yes, the album is short, but I would rather have it be short than have a longer album where I don't like half of the songs.  I like 12 of the 14 songs on this album, and I consider that to be better than most albums out there.

reviewText: After releasing two moderate selling albums, Aerosmith proved that the third time will be a charm and it did with their breakthrough classic Toys in the Attic which would sell over 6 million copies in the U.S. and score their first major hit 'Sweet Emotion'.The album begins with the pounding title track and it would become a live staple, Uncle Salty is another underrated classic, although it isn't nearly as heavy as its predecessor, it is a great song with a sing along chorus, Adam's Apple is a mid paced rocker with an excellent guitar solo and although the studio version is a great song, the live version on Pandora's Box is a killer, next up is one of Aerosmith's signature songs with 'Walk This Way' which would become a Top 10 hit and it still gets heavy classic rock airplay and another interesting note is they got the title from 'Young Frankenstein'.'Big 10'' Record' is a great song although it could've been longer, this song was a remake from like 1936, next up is another one of their signature songs called 'Sweet Emotion' which was about Steven Tyler's negative feelings about Joe Perry's soon to be wife Elissa which she is a major witch and she's the kind of person that you wouldn't like, but anyway it became Aerosmith's first breakthrough hit, 'No More No More' has great lyrics about fortune and fame and about being big, 'Round and Round' is one of Aerosmith's most creepiest songs from the 1970's and it was Brad Whitford's first song that he came up with, 'You See Me Crying' is the band's ballad and it seems like that Aerosmith would close an album with a ballad and Steven does a great job singing it.If you gotta have just one Aerosmith album, don't get Greatest Hits, instead get this album cause it rocks.

reviewText: A fivestar, wonderful, creative, excelient R&B; album by the Jacksons and the first album by the group that shows maturity with their material.  Micahel Jackson was already on fire with Off The Wall with leading singles such as "Don't Stop Till You Get Enough" and "Rock With You."  This grammy nominated, platnium #1 R&B; lp was released in 1980 and the team scored with four R&B; smashes with two of them peaking at #2 and one of them turning into a vibrant colorful video (or in Michael's words "short film") that was ignored by MTV until Michael hit big with Thriller.1. Can You Feel It - wonderful anthem song provided by excilent hooks by MJ and keyboard solo at the end of the 6 minute gem.  First saw the video on NY Hot Tracks back in the day and it is still a rarety.  A++2. Lovely One - funky part 2 of "Shake Your Body (Down To The Ground)" that was a number 2 R&B; smash and slipped out of the top ten billboard by 2 points.  Crazy hooks by MJ, punchy horns, guitar solos that gave the track spice.  This is my favorite song by the group.  Why didn't this song release a video?? This was the lps largest hit.  A++3. Your Ways - this was ok falsetto number and Jackie knows how to write, but it was not the best.  The organized horn numbers were good, but MJ's voice sounded like he was rushing for the song to end.  B-4. Everybody - this should have been a single!!  A "Get On The Floor"(from Off The Wall) replica is another party anthem that is a must listen to for a hardcore Micahel Jackson fan! - A5. This Place Hotel - art!!!  I love this song, although this was mainly a MJ solo work.  The horrorific pre-Billie Jean that opened with sister Latoya's screams started the fire into this number.  Number 2 on the R&B; charts and Number 22 on billboard charts and it use to be one of MJ's important performances on the tours from 1981's US tour with his brothers to his solo Bad Tour (1987-early 1989) A+6. Time Waits For No One - Only ballad of the album and not much effort at all.  Short but not Michael Jackson's best, but good song writing from Jackie and Randy. - C7. Walk Right Now - this "Prince"-like funky track/single was a excilent party song with dramatic, but catchy hooks by the 22 year old future king of pop.  Although no video and low positions on both charts (big mistake on such great a track), but a hit in the U.K. (good taste, U.K.!!)  "I don't care, what you're sayin'!  Walk Right Now, I ain't playin'." - excilent - A+8. Give It Up - good message song, but not as strong as "Can You Feel It." Michael gives his vocal cords some rest and lets Marlon add his part. - B+9. Wondering Who - hi-tech funky number and only song on lp that does not include Michael providing any lead vocals )although he is notable on background).  Jackie's hooks were excelient on the 4 and a half minute track.  Although this song has too many cooks (the ending of the song was kind of uneven with the synthesizers overlapping too much), it proved to be not half bad. - BI recommend any Jackson fans or hardcore classic soul lovers to purchase this cd or bid on the lp or 8 track on eBay (if you are very nolostalgic).

reviewText: A remastering of a monster album, this DUSTY IN MEMPHIS has 11 never before released tracks to add to what is already easily the best female pop album of the last 30 years.The original tracks are all classics in their  own right, and should be listened to repeatedly by anyone who wants an  expert lesson in how to sing a song.  Ms. Springfield doesn't just sing,  she inhabits every single consonant and vowel with a sense of longing,  aching sensuality and vulnerability never heard before or since.The  bonus tracks are impressive, with stand-outs being the sexy "Make It  With You" and the heavily gospel-tinged "I Found My Way."  Dusty's take on "You've Got A Friend" proves that she is and will  remain the definitive interpreter of Carole King's music.A must have for  fans, and an educational experience for a general public that has been  sadly denied exposure to the gem that is Dusty Springfield.

reviewText: I adore Eurythmics.  Any utterance from the throat of Lennox is music to my ears.  The compositions are intact with this LP.  What is lacking is the production.  Dave moved,  I blame him most,  into the Heavy Metal riffs with these instrumentations.  Having said that, "Missionary Man", "The Last Time" and "Let's Go" still hold the guitar aside the synthesizer.  The Light within the Dark isn't nullified by scratching guitars.  You'll love the grinding and electronica still used by Dave and Annie.  Overall,  a good job,  but it ain't giving me "Sweet Dreams".

reviewText: I never got into Jay-Z until "Hard Knock Life."  I just recently bought "Reasonable Doubt."  Jigga can put out quailty albums...when Jigga wants to.  Let's go down the list: Reasonable Doubt (8/10), Vol. 1 (7/10), Vol. 2 (5/10), Vol. 3 (6/10), Dynasty: Roc-la-Familia (8/10), Blueprint (9/10) and his latest release, Blueprint 2 (5.5/10).  So, it appears that when Jay-Z talked about Nas's album quality over the year's, he was also indirectly talking about his own albums, at least to me.Lyrically, Jay comes correct nine times outta ten.  For every five "Takeover's," there's at least one "'03 Bonnie & Clyde."  On "Blueprint," Jay doesn't drop the ball with lyrics.  He's on point from beginning to end.  "Takeover" is a tight battle track with Jay-Z spittin venom at Prodigy and Nas.  Everyone's heard this song, so there's no need to go into specifics.  The tightest track, lyrically, has to be "Renegade," but not because of Hova's two verses.  Eminem dropped two hot to death verses that were two of the best in 2001.Only two things keep this album from getting "five-mic" status: "Jigga That Ni**a" and "All I Need."  Production wise, these are the weak spots on the album.  Whack-masters...i mean...Track-masters produced the former, which is no more than a good club beat.  I guess i'm still bitter at Tone & Poke since the "It Was Written" debacle.  "All I Need" is an okay track, but it's neither a bump-able track or a laid-back, chillin out track.  Should've been tweaked once more before it was put on the album.In the end, people made too much of a fuss over this album being a classic.  Jay-Z has never released a "classic" album that is comparable to the likes of "Aquemini," "Illmatic," or "Enter the 36 Chambers."  To be honest, Jay is nothing more than a successful, commercialized pop rapper.  But that doesn't mean I won't blast "The Ruler's Back" down my block each day.
summary: Self-Proclaimed King Makes Good on Statement

reviewText: It seemed like Ice Cube lost a bit of credibility after starring in Are We There Yet. Before I saw it, I said that dissing Cube because of that really wasn't fair, because he had to redeem himself (although now that I HAVE seen it, it seems like it would've worked better had it been a Disney movie). When my brother asked how doing that movie could be redemption, I simply said one thing: "Did you HEAR Terrorist Threats?"But Cube came back with Laugh Now, Cry Later, an album that seems to get a little better with each listen. As other reviewers have mentioned, things start off on the right foot with the interesting "Why We Thugs". And note to the editorial reviewer: "Child Support" isn't really about that; it's a metaphor about the clichéd lyrics of young rappers. At any rate, that's also a highlight, as is the title track. "Spittin' Pollaseeds" (whatever that means) is also pretty solid, but I don't know if it's really fair to call WC a guest on that track because he's talking, not rapping.There are also a few songs I could do without, especially "Smoke Some Weed". And the filler tracks come in the form of been-there-done-that tales, like cars ("Chrome & Paint") and hardcore sex ("Steal the Show"). Furthermore, the chorus to "Growin' Up" features an out-of-place sample of Minnie Riperton's "Memory Lane". I also agree with my brother when he said that EVERYone's not waiting for another Next Friday (see the "Dimes & Nicks" skit starring Mike Epps).While not the best album Ice Cube has ever done, Laugh Now, Cry Later is still a whole lot better than a lot of the rap that's out right now. Pick it up.Anthony Rupert

reviewText: Those who thought "Songs In A-Minor" is amazing have only heard the beginning.  Many thought that its high quality could never be matched or beat.  "The Diary of Alicia Keys" beats it.  These tracks, which were written from her heart, account her personal thoughts and trials through the last two years of her life.  Her powerful words are song amazing soulful, forcing listeners to feel what she's singing.  Such quality proves that she's close to Aretha Franklin's level.  Her piano playing is equally amazing, further expressing her words.  Her combination of Motown R&B and modern day upbeats offer a unique and unmistakable sound with her songwriting.  Compared to "Songs In A-Minor", her slightly more full sound, by adding a couple extra instruments, offer the added distinction.In a time when mainstream music is released only to make money, Alicia Keys represents and gives hope to true musicians.  Obviously, she only performs because music is her passion.  This may be why her songs are much better than everyone else's.  Her talents are delivered in a variety of ways in this album: love, loneliness, sassiness, and more.  Regardless if she's singing ballads or upbeat songs, she never flaws a single note. She states with her musical quality that she'll be around for a long time.  This album will be a classic.  This is sure to please many listeners.***Expect Alicia Keys to receive at least six Grammy nominations for 2004, including Album of the Year.  She deserves them all.  She could possibly repeat her five Grammy wins for 2001.

reviewText: When this record was first released in 1980 or so, I stayed away from it: It's only big hit was "Touch and Go," which, frankly, sounded a bit weak compared with their "80's music long before the 80's" hits from their debut album and "Candy-O."What an idiot I was!Fortunately, I bought this record (yes, 33-1/3 vinyl) almost a decade later because, although I'm idiot, I am also a completist.So, expecting an album with a so-so hit and a lot of filler, I instead discovered a killer album, on which any song could easily fit in with the likes of "Good Times Roll," "Dangerous Type" and "Shake It Up." For an album that was purportedly filler, the only filler song I found on it was the record's only hit, "Touch and Go." How's that for irony?Unlike other reviewers, I lack the capacity to categorize the songs into "guitar rockers," "new wave tunes" and "electronic synth," or whatever other ones there are. To me, that is bside the point, because Cars music is such a deft blend of all three of these, for any song you choose to pick.The album's best tunes (which is difficult, since there are nine totally solid cuts), in order of my favorites: "Misfit Kid," "Gimme Some Slack," "Running to You," "Up and Down."Peculiar favorite: "Down Boys." Ric Ocasek had a unique voice, but no one could sing as convincingly as bassist Benjamin Orr. I remember the mid-80's well, and there was no quicker way to bed a girl than by putting "Drive" on the turntable. He had that Sinatra thing going for him.Most prophetic song: "Getting Through."Check out these lyrics:"With the circus mouths shooting all directions /"And TV ads that sell erections"(15 years before Viagra, easy)"I don't want to be your bad connection /"Fit into your reality vision"(All the merde on TV today, from "Survivor," "The Apprentice" and "Fear Factor")The Cars were the ultimate 80's band. By this one and get transported back to a better decade, long before prefab boy bands and lip-synching girls with silicone chests monopolized the sorry remains of pop music.

reviewText: THE END OF THE INNOCENCE was Don Henley's third solo album and his second since he signed with Geffen Records. Five years later,this album was released. Henley had two previous megahits with The Eagles,their albums HOTEL CALIFORNIA and THE LONG RUN. Other hits include THE LAST WORTHLESS EVENING,I WILL NOT GO QUIETLY,THE HEART OF THE MATTER and NEW YORK MINUTE. GIMME WHAT YOU GOT features Geffen Records labelmate Edie Brickell singing background(I want it,I want it). NEW YORK MINUTE also appeared on the Eagles' reunion concert album HELL FREEZES OVER,released in 1994. All the other tracks are good.

reviewText: Of all the excellent albums the Ohio Players recorded for Mercury Records in the mid-70's this, their debut for the label is without a doubt in my mind the best. Is' a classic an' established the Dayton funksters as one'a the best bands of the decade. Erotic album covers, rubbery bass grooves an' horn sections, sweaty, thumpin' basslines, hell, it embodies the very definition of funk. The title track an' 'Jive Turkey' are down an' dirty funk classics, and even though they stretch on for over seven minutes, the basslines an' funky intertwined guitars an' keyboards somehow don't get old, an' allow you to just let it run. This is especially true on the jazz-influenced 'Heaven Must Be Like This', an absolutely excellent and stunning ballad that will ALWAYS be my joint. It was memorably covered by D'Angelo on his rarely-heard live album, but even his amazing talent can't compare to Sugarfoot an' the crew's angelic and captivatingly romantic tones on the song. This was one of the songs me an' my baby danced to on our first date an' I would have loved to have been trapped in that moment forever. Trust me, the Players' excellent balladry isn't discussed nearly enough. The production here is tight, clear, but never overly-polished. It's still bass-heavy, dirty, sweaty an' downright NASTY funk; e'ything you'd expect from 'em.

reviewText: Bon Iver's sophomore album has the distinction of being not only indie-rock kids' most anticipated efforts of 2011, but one of the year's MOST anticipated efforts, period.  After contributing vocals to Kanye West's critical and commercial darlingMy Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasyin 2010, Bon Iver's stock greatly rose, making the ever inquisitive, curious music enthusiast (moi) curious of the artists and his sophomore release. Having never heard Bon Iver's debutFor Emma, Forever Ago, a critical darling and favorite among indie circles (or so I am told), I won't compare 2011'sBon Iverto anything but will judge it only as its own entity.  That stated, Bon Iver is a flawed album with some extraordinarily capable and credible moments.  The biggest flaw of Bon Iver is the ponderousness and sometimes emptiness of the material, which promotes more timbre and production over songwriting and structure.  If this album were judge solely on its sound arrangements and the grand and sparsity of the production work, it would be nearly flawless.  However, too many instances production and timbre take precedence over the `song' itself, which hurts Bon Iver ever so slightly."Perth" opens up the album spacey, but beautifully with acoustic guitars.  Throughout, some memorable guitar riffs nudge their head bringing a sense of unity to the cut.  The snare drum work here is notable, serving as support for frontman Justin Vernon's vocal experiments.  Why "Perth" works so well is it's simplicity and creativity with sounds (timbre).  Follow-up cut "Minnesota, WI" isn't too shabby, though the `structure' of the song is perhaps too ambitious or devoid of a more accessible form.  Sure, this is `indie-rock' (despite the incredible numbers Bon Iver opened with), but still a few more hints to the listener as far as structure would have put "Minnesota, WI" over-the-top. On a positive note, Vernon sounds great exploiting his lower singing register, and the use of varied sounds is superb (saxophones, guitars, synthesizer, banjo, etc.)  "Holocene" steals the show from both "Perth" and "Minnesota, WI," introducing the bizarre use of vibraphone and at times bowed vibraphone, usually more at home in either a jazz or  wind ensemble/orchestra setting.  Additionally, the use of reeds in tandem with one another (saxophones, clarinet) is sheer genius. Besides an excellently penned chorus ("and at once I knew I was not magnificent...I could see for miles, miles, miles..."), the songwriting as whole is among the best of the entire effort."Towers" isn't bad, and the opening guitars dictate a faster tempo than the slower pace set by the first three cuts.  The pedal steel is a wonderful addition to the overall timbre here and marks a high point of this cut.  Additionally, the use of acoustic instruments is so nice (and rare) to hear, even sometimes on indie releases.  The quibble would be that "Towers" is a better `concept' than `song.' "Michicant" atones `big-time' with a nice six-feel established from the onset, contrasting the groove of previous cuts.  The vocal production surround Vernon's voice here sounds particularly well done here.  As far as the mix and production, it is some of the most refined and skilled of the album.  The most brilliant moment might be during Vernon's third verse, when two separate sets of saxophones are panned to the left and to the right.  "Hinnom, TX" is conceptual, but lacks being a true `song' as opposed to merely a `soundscape'; James Blake's self-titled debut effort (James Blake) similarly suffers from the ails Bon Iver suffers at times.  "Wash." saves the day (and is arguably the second-best cut), featuring a superb, tender vocal performance by Vernon, oft-times accompanied by piano with use of strings (violin, viola) and pedal steel.  The harmonized vocals are a high point for certain.The final three cuts of Bon Iver are disappointing, causing the effort to sag and lose some of its zest.  "Calgary" sounds a bit too nebulous, lacking enough structure to truly allure or captivate its listener.  "Lisbon, OH" serves it purpose as an instrumental cut, but given the averageness of "Calgary," it fails to rebuild support as Bon Iver tumbles the slightest bit.  Closing cut "Beth/Rest" cannot compare to the best cuts of the album ("Perth," "Holocene," "Michicant," or "Wash.") and it closes the album less satisfactorily than it opened.Overall,Bon Iveris a flawed affair with some truly genius moments. Perhaps with some extra attention, Bon Iver could have been an even better affair.  Nonetheless, hardcore Bon Iver fans will be happy to add this effort next to For Emma, Forever Ago, even it underwhelms at times.
summary: A Flawed Album With Some Brilliant Moments
filteredReviewText: Bon Iver's sophomore album has the distinction of being not only indie-rock kids' most anticipated efforts of 2011, but one of the year's MOST anticipated efforts, period. After contributing vocals to Kanye West's critical and commercial darlingMy Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasyin 2010, Bon Iver's stock greatly rose, making the ever inquisitive, curious music enthusiast (moi) curious of the artists and his sophomore release. Having never heard Bon Iver's debutFor Emma, Forever Ago, a critical darling and favorite among indie circles (or so I am told), I won't compare 2011'sBon Iverto anything but will judge it only as its own entity. That stated, Bon Iver is a flawed album with some extraordinarily capable and credible moments. The biggest flaw of Bon Iver is the ponderousness and sometimes emptiness of the material, which promotes more timbre and production over songwriting and structure. If this album were judge solely on its sound arrangements and the grand and sparsity of the production work, it would be nearly flawless. However, too many instances production and timbre take precedence over the `song' itself, which hurts Bon Iver ever so slightly."Perth" opens up the album spacey, but beautifully with acoustic guitars. Throughout, some memorable guitar riffs nudge their head bringing a sense of unity to the cut. The snare drum work here is notable, serving as support for frontman Justin Vernon's vocal experiments. Why "Perth" works so well is it's simplicity and creativity with sounds (timbre). Follow-up cut "Minnesota, WI" isn't too shabby, though the `structure' of the song is perhaps too ambitious or devoid of a more accessible form. Sure, this is `indie-rock' (despite the incredible numbers Bon Iver opened with), but still a few more hints to the listener as far as structure would have put "Minnesota, WI" over-the-top. On a positive note, Vernon sounds great exploiting his lower singing register, and the use of varied sounds is superb (saxophones, guitars, synthesizer, banjo, etc.) "Holocene" steals the show from both "Perth" and "Minnesota, WI," introducing the bizarre use of vibraphone and at times bowed vibraphone, usually more at home in either a jazz or wind ensemble/orchestra setting. Besides an excellently penned chorus ("and at once I knew I was not magnificent...I could see for miles, miles, miles..."), the songwriting as whole is among the best of the entire effort."Towers" isn't bad, and the opening guitars dictate a faster tempo than the slower pace set by the first three cuts. The pedal steel is a wonderful addition to the overall timbre here and marks a high point of this cut. Additionally, the use of acoustic instruments is so nice (and rare) to hear, even sometimes on indie releases. The quibble would be that "Towers" is a better `concept' than `song.' "Michicant" atones `big-time' with a nice six-feel established from the onset, contrasting the groove of previous cuts. The vocal production surround Vernon's voice here sounds particularly well done here. As far as the mix and production, it is some of the most refined and skilled of the album. The most brilliant moment might be during Vernon's third verse, when two separate sets of saxophones are panned to the left and to the right. "Hinnom, TX" is conceptual, but lacks being a true `song' as opposed to merely a `soundscape' saves the day (and is arguably the second-best cut), featuring a superb, tender vocal performance by Vernon, oft-times accompanied by piano with use of strings (violin, viola) and pedal steel. The harmonized vocals are a high point for certain.The final three cuts of Bon Iver are disappointing, causing the effort to sag and lose some of its zest. "Calgary" sounds a bit too nebulous, lacking enough structure to truly allure or captivate its listener. "Lisbon, OH" serves it purpose as an instrumental cut, but given the averageness of "Calgary," it fails to rebuild support as Bon Iver tumbles the slightest bit. Closing cut "Beth/Rest" cannot compare to the best cuts of the album ("Perth," "Holocene," "Michicant," or "Wash.") and it closes the album less satisfactorily than it opened.Overall,Bon Iveris a flawed affair with some truly genius moments. Perhaps with some extra attention, Bon Iver could have been an even better affair.

reviewText: Razorlight's third release,Slipway Fires, has a strong traditional rock flavor to the album.  I can only guess this was intended to broaden their appeal and make them accessible to those who traditionally don't listen to alternative rock.  In fact, most of this album is what I would call just plain old rock until you reach the sixth track, "60 Thompson."  There is nothing wrong with that, but Razorlight fans, such as myself, who were looking forward to the raw energy of their other albums may be left scratching their heads with this one.  This album has some good songs on it, but it feels more like a collection of songs than a coherent album.  Even though it has grown on me, I prefer songs on their other albums to this one.  I even prefer the second album, which has been put down a lot.  Even though this album has a much higher quality production to it, it feels like something was lost in the process of cleaning them up for this release.There are a lot of songs on this album that sound like other bands.  "You & The Rest" has aViolent Femmessort of feel to it.  The first part of "Tabloid Lover" is reminiscent of earlyTalking Heads, but the Chorus sounds more like the early Beatles.  "Stinger" sounds more like theMoody Blues, and "Burberry Blue Eyes" could have easily been anElvis Costellocover.  "Blood For Wild Blood" sounds like a hybrid betweenINXS&U2sung over a church organ.  In fact the last track sounds so much like aBilly Joelsong I had to check the writing credits.  I didn't like all these songs the first time around but a few of them grew on me.Track 10, "Monster Boots," sounded most like what I expected to hear from Razorlight, and it's probably my favorite track on this album.  I also like "60 Thompson" though I did feel like it was almost too short.  Even "Hostage of Love" grew on me, and that song proves that not everything on this album is mellow.  Even though I enjoy a lot of those classic sounding tracks, only a few of them will make it onto my personal playlists.I will definitely buy Razorlight's next album, but I hope they get back some of the raw energy they seem to have relinquished with this release.  You can use various sites to preview these songs before buying this album, and this might be a case where you will be better served to download the tracks you like instead of buying the whole album.  As somebody who usually buys a lot of albums, that's a painful recommendation for me to make about a band I like.  I do think that those who like mainstream rock more than alternative may find this album to be a palatable cross-over introduction.Enjoy.

reviewText: ...not quite 5-star material in my opinion. This is a beautiful pop achievement in these days of fewer-and-farther-between catchy melodies. Previous reviewers are spot on in noting that Travis' style is somewhere  between The Verve and Radiohead -- Fran Healy's vocals bear a close  resemblance to Thom Yorke and, yes, David Gates of 70's popsters Bread.  Despite a few tedious, if not uninspired moments, this album gets better  with every listen ... at first listen I was ready to dismiss them as  Radiohead knockoffs. Yet, unforgettable pop gems like "Writing to  Reach You", "Driftwood", "Turn" and, of course,  "Why Does It Always Rain on Me?" make this an album not to be  missed. Here's hoping they continue to gain their due recognition and  evolve a style of their own.

reviewText: The first version of the Jeff Beck Group existed in a transitional period in time, before bands like The Faces and Led Zeppelin came into being, and after Jeff Beck's ejection from the Yardbirds. It's all in the timing because it also followed the folding of bands like the Shotgun Express and the Birds, from which he recruited Rod Stewart and Ron Wood, then both still relatively unknown. Mick Waller on drums had known Rod Stewart from earlier Steampacket days and came to the band from the Brian Auger Trinity.Truth was the first album by the group although it was released under the name Jeff Beck, who was simultaneously "enjoying" a solo career, masterminded by producer Mickie Most, and having hits with songs such as Hi Ho Silver Lining, Tallyman and Love Is Blue (shudder).The truer heart of Jeff Beck was to be found on the B-sides and on this debut album, which was mostly left to Ken Scott, the engineer, to handle, whilst Mickie Most no doubt dreamt of one day discovering elfin girls in black leather cat suits with bass guitars.After eighteen months of grafting on the road the band were pretty hot. It is a classic album, though the shortage of material does show, with versions of Ol' Man River and a throwaway filler in Greensleeves. This was inspired by Chet Atkins' version, though Mick Waller had previously recorded a rocked-up version of it for Joe Meek with the Flee-Rekkers back in 1960 as Green Jeans. Carrying on that tradition, several of the tracks are thinly disguised rewrites of well-known blues songs. Let Me Love You is essentially Buddy Guy's Let Me Love You Baby; Rock My Plimsoul is clearly BB King's Rock Me Baby (although BB himself nicked it from Lil' Son Jackson) and Blues De Luxe owes more than a little to BB's Gambling Blues.There's also a reworking of Shapes Of Things, a Yardbirds hit that Jeff played on; a cover of Tim Rose's arrangement of Morning Dew; a version of Muddy Waters' You Shook Me with John Paul Jones (soon to be of Led Zeppelin) guesting on Hammond; and a rip-roaring rendition of Willie Dixon's I Ain't Superstitious, as recorded by the great Howlin' Wolf.The album set a sort of blueprint for a genre that came to be known as heavy rock, made possible by developments in the technology of electrical musical instruments, amplification and recording equipment, of which Jeff and his sidemen were early adopters and experimenters. In the Yardbirds, of course, he had been a pioneer of feedback. The sound was developed on the second album,Beck-Ola, but with less light and shade than is found on Truth.Rounding out the album is the instrumental Beck's Bolero, an earlier recording from July 1966. It had previously appeared on the B-side of Hi Ho Silver Lining and has the unique line-up supporting Jeff of Jimmy Page (12-string electric guitar), Nicky Hopkins (keyboards), John Paul Jones (bass) and Keith Moon (drums)! The tune is credited to Jimmy Page, though Maurice Ravel may have had a hand in it. On the album it is shorn of the backwards guitar part at the end but is newly mixed into rudimentary stereo.This edition of the CD comes with 16 pages of booklet notes including an informative essay by Charles Shaar Murray, and a number of bonus tracks (all stereo except where stated): I've Been Drinking had been the B-side of Love Is Blue, and so was unlikely to have been heard by legions of Jeff Beck fans who would have avoided the single like the plague, and was an adaptation of Dinah Washington's Drinking Again. There are the first takes of All Shook Up and Blues De Luxe, the latter without the fake live effects that were overdubbed to the eventual master; the excellent 1967 single Tallyman (in mono) and its B-side, an earlier recording of Rock My Plimsoul, both from a time when Aynsley Dunbar was the drummer; and Hi Ho Silver Lining, first recorded by the Attack, and its B-side, the original mono, backward guitar mix of Bolero.Finally, it includes the dreaded Love Is Blue (in mono). Where to begin with this blot in Jeff Beck's discography? It began life as L'Amour Est Bleu by the Paul Mauriat Orchestra, and with words added became Luxembourg's 1967 entry in the Eurovision Song Contest as sung by Vicky Leandros. It came fourth but was popular enough to be recorded by the likes of Andy Williams and Claudine Longet. It falls way outside Jeff Beck's comfort zone and suggests that Mickie Most must have had a very persuasive tongue.

reviewText: Okay, to start off, "Snakes and Arrows" is not the return to form that old fans still pining for the sequel to "2112" have been wanting for decades. That Rush is long gone. And that is not a bad thing. Rush has never been a band that does the same thing over and over, or a band that wants to revisit the past, so why should they start now?On to the new record...it is a grower. It has some of the best melodies they have written in a long time, Neil Peart's lyrics are still as potent as ever, and, to the delight of this listener, there is more acoustic guitar than on any other Rush album to date.From a playing standpoint, this is Alex Lifeson's record. No, he does not dazzle us with solos left and right, although there are a few nice ones, but his playing throughout the record is top-notch. Some have called him the weak link in the band before, usually because of how prolific his bandmates are, but he owns "Snakes and Arrows." Geddy Lee and Neil Peart do their usual great job, too, don't get me wrong, but Lifeson's star shines the brightest.As I mentioned earlier, this album is a grower. The more you listen to it, the more those melodies get in your head, and before you know it, you can't get the cd out of your disc player. Every song is at least good, and quite a few range from very good to great, especially "Armor and Sword," "Bravest Face," "The Way the Wind Blows," "The Main Monkey Business," and "Malignant Narcissism."Is is their best album ever? No. Is it their best album since "Moving Pictures," their classic from 1981? No. But it is a very good record, and for a bunch of guys in their 50's, who have been together for over 30 years, it is awfully impressive.

reviewText: Though it took her a while to completely win me over (as I am not a particular fan of her vocal style), Fantasia Barrino is undoubtedly talented. Memorable moments from the third season of American Idol, which Fantasia won, included her first words after winning ("I broke my shoe!"), her energetic performances, and of course her rendition of "Summertime". Fantasia's debut, "Free Yourself", takes on a more urban sound, which does not necessarily suit her voice. She enlists the help of many hitmakers, including Missy Elliott, Jermaine Dupri and Darkchild, which goes to show that Fantasia is taking a different approach than other Idol winners (who enlisted writers like Diane Warren and Babyface on their albums). However, having the right producers does not help if the singer cannot back them up. It's not that Fantasia has a weak voice or anything of that nature. She simply is not really suited for this style. True, a lot of her performances on American Idol were upbeat and energetic, but she really shined on her ballads.First up is "Ain't Gon' Beg You" which talks about a man who treated Fantasia wrong and how she's tired of begging. The song is not all that impressive. Fantasia's vocals are on point however the song seems to be missing something. Lyrically, it is merely average. The title, "Free Yourself" is up next, in which Fantasia tells her man that if he doesn't want to be in the relationship, he should "go ahead and free [him]self". The chorus is extremely repetitive and this entire song seems below what we know Fantasia is capable of. The first truly stunning track comes in the form of "Truth Is", a song about running into someone from your past and realizing you still have feelings for him. Lyrically, it is simple yet touching and although Fantasia doesn't do anything particularly impressive with her vocals, she manages to convey a lot of emotion that only makes the song more touching."Selfish (I Want You To Myself)" is much more upbeat than any of the previous songs. It features a weak (lyrically) rap from Missy Elliott and is otherwise fairly average. At times however it seems to suit Fantasia pretty well though if you really break it down, it is no different from any other song these days. "Summertime" is up next, and of course is an album highlight. Though it's a remake, Fantasia makes it her own and gives her best vocal performance. The only problem with this song is that it is too short as it lasts just over two and half minutes. Although "Baby Mama" had good intentions, it fails to be really anything interesting, especially since Fantasia spells out the title multiple times in the song. While it's good of Fantasia to dedicate a song to all of the single mothers (like herself), it could have been done so much better."Got Me Waiting" carries on in the same vein as "Ain't Gon' Beg You" though it is not much better lyrically. At least this song has some good, but subdued vocals. Other than that, it is not all that memorable and tends to blend in with the rest of the album. "It's All Good" (a highly overused phrase) is another upbeat song, which uses the fairly overused "handclap" background. The song seems to be made for the clubs but surprisingly enough, it is not too bad until it gets to the chorus. ("It's all good, I don't care that you broke my heart.") It seems a little odd for Fantasia to be singing lyrics like these immediately after talking about not putting up with cheating men. "Good Lovin'" is a bit more like what one would expect from Fantasia. It is a mid-tempo song with quieter background music. This would allow Fantasia's vocals to shine however she sings instead in a subdued manner to match the music, thus not really letting us hear her talent. Fantasia could have done so much more with this song."Don't Act Right" is a fairly standard song about a man who cheats Fantasia badly. Fantasia once again does not live up to her potential, and instead settles for singing more quietly and so the song tends to blend with the rest of the album. "You Were Always On My Mind" is another remake as well as another highlight. Fantasia shows off her vocals on this one, reminding listeners why she won in the first place. This song is quite impressive and allows Fantasia's talent to truly shine through. "This Is Me" probably would have been great had Fantasia not repeated that she was from the ghetto so many times. It seems the writers were trying to drill it into our heads where Fantasia came from though that does nothing to improve the song. Lastly, there is "I Believe" which was written by Tamyra Gray and is an amazing way to finish off the album. This is definitely one of the more powerful songs on the album and Fantasia truly shows off her talent once more.Overall Mark: 3/5It wasn't until Fantasia sang "Summertime" on American Idol that I really realized how talented she was. Unfortunately, this album does little to show that talent. Fantasia tries hard to fit in with modern, urban R&B; and in the process hides her voice behind the production. Also, the material on the album (with some exceptions) did absolutely nothing to prove Fantasia as an artist. Most of it is fairly bland but is saved by Fantasia's voice. Even when she does not sing as well as most of us know she can, she manages to turn a potentially weak song into something better. "Summertime", "I Believe", "You Were Always On My Mind" and "Truth Is" remain the only truly great songs. The rest range from subpar to average. As a whole, I expected a lot more from this album and it is likely that with the right writers and producers, Fantasia could have delivered.

reviewText: In The City introduced The Jam as a brash young hipster band with one foot in the UK punk underground and the other in America's R&B past.  Then came This Is The Modern World, a rushed attempt at cash-in success that failed.  Then All Mod Cons, a typical Jam album, solid if unspectacular.  Setting Sons, the pseudo-concept album followed with its poppy sounds and glossy production.  Then, the skies parted, and Sound Affects was bestowed upon the world, and everything was perfect.Weller's poetic/sarcastic wit combine with edgy but poppy tunes to really make this The Jam's standout album.  I don't believe there is a bad song on the album, and at least 3 songs (Pretty Green, That's Entertainment, & Man In The Corner Shop) rank among the best they've ever done.  It's a top-notch album that deserves a lot more notoriety than it receives.  Though the sad truth is that it was all downhill for The Jam after this one.And though I can't say they were better than The Clash (The Only Band That Matters, even after all these years) The Jam were better than most.  This CD proves it.  An undisputed classic.

reviewText: With their third release, Godsmack really shines, harder and better than ever before. A strong, radio-ready hit opens the album with "Straight Out of Line". Godsmack continues the energy rise with the next two tracks, "Faceless", and "Changes". And perhaps the most powerful song they've ever recorded comes into play at #5, "I Stand Alone", in my opinion, one of the best heavy rock songs ever recorded. They continue the awesome song trend with "Re-Align", a softer side where the lyrics absolutely shine. Next, a throwback to their debut with "I F*****g Hate You", an angry song that bristles with tension and malice. Another stand-out is "I Am", in which lead singer Sully Erna declares "death will come when i'm good and God d**n ready". And Godsmack does it again with the melodic, almost tribal "Serenity", where the chanting chorus can make your heart pump with intensity. Overall, this is their best record yet and an excellent purchase. This album apppeals to all rock fans who love quality music. An awesome album.

reviewText: With the exception of Yes, Steely Dan is generally the closest I come to prog-rock. So if you think I don't really know the genre, you're right. However, I feel this is overblown and pretentious. Granted, all that can't stop Nights In White Satin from being an incredibly powerful, lovely piece (other than the crappy stoner poem at the end). But even then, it doesn't strike me like the work of Yes (specifically Close to the Edge and Starship Trooper). The rest is overblown and endless, especially all eight-and-a-half minutes of the aptly-titled Forever Afternoon. If you're looking for grade "A" prog-rock, go with Yes.

reviewText: You can't overstate the impact of Kurt Cobain and Nirvana. Five great albums is the obvious contribution that he made, and can you believe almost twenty years ago. But the even better bi-product is, bands you may have never heard got major exposure thanks to connection to Cobain.The Melvins used Cobain as drummer and producer. They also stewed  noise and punk and metal, like artist barbarians in ripped T-shirts, long before people converted from big hair to flannel. Take Black Sabbath and a cartoon take on Captain Beefheart noise, splash it on a wall, and you have a starting concept of the Melvins. Not a drop of Quiet Motly Crew Riot Poison , or production gloss, within miles.  It took Cobain to over throw the entire 1980s for the public to catch up to a band that lived on a planet with no  MTV rock and just did not care.I don't know a lot of this band's work but each album I buy, upon finding, impresses me.Melvinsfor its mudpie of noise and slam, and Houdini for its straightforward take on some seriously heavy steel and iron. The singer hear actually has the band sounding a little like Metalica, if that band stripped away the big production and all persona. Great tight songs, slamming guitars, slow motion primal rage,  all recorded in the toolshed.You can argue my comparisons, you can argue my history. But when metal is stripped of all the trimmings, and there is just the noise and the sound, you can't deny the sheer power of the music, or Houdini

reviewText: Just to let everyone know, I really rate this album @ 3 1/2 stars (you would think Amazon would've implemented a rating system that allowed for halves...hint hint, Amazon!). Moving along, I'm a Ghostface fan, hands down; I started backwards: I fell in love with "The Pretty Toney Album," went back and copped "Supreme Clientele" (which I borrowed from a high school buddy so much to the point it was almost mine), and decided to go for his joint "that went wood" (that's a quote from the second verse of the last song on "Pretty Toney Album").Again, being a huge Ghostface fan, I have to admit, "Bulletproof Wallets" was not his best work, and after listening to it a few times, it's easy to see why this album was basically UNHEARD OF (heck, I didn't even know Ghost had dropped this). Compared to his other work, it's lackluster -- it doesn't suck, but if it weren't for Ghost's ALWAYS on point vocal delivery, it would definitely have suffered an immense loss for an incredible emcee."Bulletproof Wallets" doesn't even seem to fit in between the AWESOME "Supreme Clientele" and dope "Pretty Toney" - I'm scratching my head! In my opinion, most of the beats are either lackluster, or just aren't fit for the type of darts Ghost throws. LACKLUSTER PRODUCTION: "Maxine;" "Flowers;" "Never Be the Same Again;" "Love Session" - And in terms of the last two aforementioned songs, what's with the R&B; crap? To quote RZA from the Second Disc Intro on "Wu-Tang Forever," this is hip hop, not R&B;: "...Rap & Bulls***."Dope cuts are "Ghost Showers" (the radio single for this album, which is like a sequel to "Cherchez la Ghost," but doesn't even come close), "Strawberry," "The Forest," and the two Alchemist joints "The Juks" and "Street Chemistry," the latter which should've been longer than one and a half minutes!!! ARGHHH! Don't you hate that? (SEE: "Invocation" from Common's "One Day It'll All Make Sense")The verdict? If you're a Ghost fan and have to have this to complete your collection, then you'll appreciate the dope cuts, possibly overlooking the mediocrity that plagues most of this album. If you're not a fan or Ghost is more of a "listen to him when he's on" cat, "Bulletproof Wallets" is going to suck to you. I think my money would've stretched longer purchasing the first joint, "Ironman." Honestly, Ghost's fans can't be blamed for "sleepin" on this one. PEACE!

reviewText: Almost all the attention goes to the A side, with "Heads Will Roll" and "Soft Shock," but the majestic, ethereal beauty of this album is locked in on the B side, which brings together all the strands in the minds of the Yeah Yeah Yeahs -- american girl group, english girl group, the Cure, space rock, dreampop, huge soundscapes washing over tiny vistas -- and delivers one of the great extended pop listens of our time. The hooks and melodies are classic pop and gorgeous and keep the huge sound from drifting off into some kind or torpid, bloated bore. It's beautifully focussed and realized and I would emphasize that it shows master craftspeople at their work if that wouldn't distract from the nicest part: Despite her favored space face, our girl can be exceedingly human. (bonus points for the clean and vivid vinyl, which I recommend)

reviewText: Junior M.A.F.I.A.'s first album from 1995 had a few good numbers, but most of this album is uneven.  It sounds like it was recorded on a New York subway in Brooklyn and wasn't quite finished.  The Get Money song has that '70s thing going on in it, as with most of the songs with the samples. Lil' Kim, Lil' Cease and Notorious B.I.G's parts are all good and were the best rappers in the group.  It's smart that Kim branched out into a solo career a year later and has made 3 albums. The lyrics on money, cars, jewelry go into overkill on many of the songs. The remaining members say that they're making a new album. I hope it's better than this disjointed, uneven album that came and went in 6 months.

reviewText: In many band's cases, the band's final album is usually said to be one of the band's finest albums. Unfortunately, in Jefferson Airplane's case, I can't say that. 'Long John Silver' is weak under Jefferson Airplane's standards.It's 1972. Marty Balin has since departed from the group, leaving only Paul Kantner, Grace Slick and guitarist Jorma Kaukonen left to handle the vocal duties. Jefferson Airplane's previous album, 1971's 'Bark,' wasn't strong as far as Airplane records go, and it didn't help that Balin had left the band.So, the group issues 'Long John Silver.' This record is good as far as albums from the time go, but one would have a hard time telling this was the same Jefferson Airplane that released 'Surrealistic Pillow' a couple years earlier.But it's not all that bad. 'Eat Starch Mom' and the title track are very strong, and are actually really good. I have always considered the title track to be early '70s punk, just because of the drumming and Kaukonen's guitar.Overall, if you are a casual Airplane, definitely skip this in favor of some of their earlier studio albums and/or their compilation albums. This isn't a terrible album, but one would expect better from a band like Jefferson Airplane.Recommended, but only for Jefferson Airplane collectors.

Jefferson Airplane's previous album, 1971's 'Bark,' wasn't strong as far as Airplane records go, and it didn't help that Balin had left the band.So, the group issues 'Long John Silver.' one would have a hard time telling this was the same Jefferson Airplane that released 'Surrealistic Pillow' a couple years earlier.But it's not all that bad. 'Eat Starch Mom' and the title track are very strong, and are actually really good. I have always considered the title track to be early '70s punk, just because of the drumming and Kaukonen's guitar.Overall, if you are a casual Airplane, definitely skip this in favor of some of their earlier studio albums and/or their compilation albums. This isn't a terrible album, but one would expect better from a band like Jefferson Airplane.Recommended, but only for Jefferson Airplane collectors.

reviewText: Will this album ever sound dated? Let's hope not. In 1971, Motown's first certified sex symbol cast off the burden of being a hit making-machine and transformed himself into a true artist. "What's Going On" forever  shattered the myth that R&B albums were simply a couple of hit singles  packaged together with a few filler cuts thrown in to balance things out.  This was (and is) simply revolutionary. From Marvin's appearance during  that era, (the longer hair, full beard, skull caps and warm-ups) to the  packaging of the product (detailed liner notes and the somber cover art)  there really has never, before or since, been anything to rival the musical  or social impact of this release. The music, of course, hasn't aged a day.  Dominated by the sound of Gaye's wondrously multi-tracked voice, the album  isn't rushed, and clocking in at just under 40 minutes, it isn't so long it  starts to bore the listener. Though it features only 9 tracks, the flawless  sequencing and jazzy,languid pace of the songs gives it the feel of a  sprawling epic, most notable on "Right On". Trying to divide this  into separate songs is pretty much an exercise in futility since this was  obviously intended as a suite, not a "hits" collection. The  opening title track has become a perrenial radio favorite and followed by  the equally stirring "What's Happening Brother", the tone is  initially one of sorrow and awareness of how the world around us is  decaying. My favorite section of this masterpiece is "Flying High in  The Friendly Sky" a dreamy meditation on Marvin's use of mind altering  chemicals( 'So stupid minded, I can't help it, But I go crazy when I can't  find it") that leaves the listener drifting in it's haze. "Mercy  Mercy Me (The Ecology), will not only prick your heart with it's depiction  of the enviroment's destruction, but the music (orchestra, chior, James  Jamerson's outstanding bass playing, the congas echoing in the back) and  Marvin's understated vocals, are wonders unto themselves. I could go on  forever about this album but words alone simply can't do it justice, you  must hear it for yourself. And if you haven't already, what planet have you  been living on? No matter what format you find it on, vinyl, CD or  cassette, get it, your life and the way you hear all other music be forever  altered. Though he's been gone from us for over 16 years now, Marvin Gaye  still casts a long shadow over all of popular music and many singers, young  and old, black and white have tried in vain to recapture some of his magic.  His genius was unparalelled, and if he had never recorded again after  "What's Going On", his place in history was already secured. This  album is a national treasure, no collection is complete without it.

reviewText: Alice's best and most consistent album. The hit title track only scratches the surface, the rest hold up to that standard. reviewText: Like everyone else I have been waiting for this album. Paula went through her ups and downs in the off years. She had a child and had her heart broken. The joy and pain is sprinkled throughout this album. This is by far the best Paula Cole album ever released. Paula's love of jazz which was seen sparingly on past albums is the main force behind "Courage".from the inside jacket:"That anyone is holding this album in their hands, reading these words, is a small miracle....I didn't want to be in the business anymore. I was too broken-hearted about it, investigating University enrollment, or considering the life of a hermit...Through the music, I have found myself again."Well, Paula, thank YOU for returning to the business and blessing my ears with this jewel of an album.

reviewText: This is almost a "super-Exit Stage Left" -- the band's most popular tunes, some more recent material, with an additional disc of previously unreleased live material from 1978.  The sound here is good though it lacks the sparkling, overly doctored sound of Exit Stage Left. It's nice to have some of the more recent material live (especially "Dreamline", "Show Don't Tell", and "Bravado") and there are also some previously unreleased classics, like the "2112" suite (edited on All the World's a Stage), "Natural Science", and an amazing "Analog Kid".  The 1978 disc is leagues ahead of All the World's a Stage, with most of the material from A Farewell to Kings performed really well.  I'm not sure whether it was necessary to include "Tom Sawyer", "Closer to the Heart", and other hits on yet another live album, but this is still a great value for 3 CDs.  Definitely the band's best release of the 90s and worth buying for Rush fans.

reviewText: It's hard to believe that there was a time when there was no Jay-hova, Jigga my N***a, or Jay-Z the god mc.  Jay-Z burst onto the hip hop scene with this classic album. When he dropped this album he proved that he was going to be one of hip-hop's mainstays.  In my opinion, this is tied for the best hiphop album of all time with Biggie's Life After Death.  Following them would be Nas - Illmatic and Snoop Dogg's Doggystyle.On the first track, Can't Knock the Hustle, all of Jigga's verses are straight fire!!  With Mary J on the chorus, things don't get much better than this.  The next track Politics as Usual comes off as a hot track as well.  Now this next track is one of the best songs of the 90s.  I'm talking about Brooklyn's Finest.  On this track produced by DJ Clark Kent, Jay teams up with Biggie Smalls to deliver another track that is on fire!!  Think about it, the two greatest rappers ever on a track together.  My favorite line is when Biggie says:If Faith had twins she'd probably have 2 pacsGet it two Pacs . . .Now this next track Dead Presidents II, is one of my favorite Jay-Z tracks ever.  This one is so good that there's not much to say except that it is fire.  Jay sampled the voice of Nas on this one and made a classic song.  Not to mention that Ski hooked Jay up with one of the best beats in hip-hop history.Feelin' It was one of the singles for the album and it is a hot track too.  The next track is called D'evils.  Many people may not agree with me, but D'evils is one of the best tracks on the album.  For you to understand why I say this then you have to go back and listen to Jay's lines closely.D'Evils - "Thinking back when we first learned to use rubbersHe never learned so in turn I'm kidnapping his baby's motherMy hand around her collar, feeding her cheese...Those lines were incredible.Check out the track 22 two's.  Jay is freestyling in a club and Ski laces him with another dope beat.  Pay close attention and you'll realize that he says the word too, 22 times.  Hence the name of the track.  His next track Can I Live is another fire track.  Damn Jigga rips this track.  On Can I Live Jay said"dreams of getting cheese, it gets te-di-ous, so I keep one eye open like CBS"On Ain't No N---a, Jay is with Foxy Brown talking about sex.  It's not fire, but is still a very hot track.Next is Friend of Foe and even though it's short, it still comes off as hot.  On Coming of Age Jay-Z introduces his protege Memphis Bleek and this track is pretty good too.  These verses by Bleek are some of the best he's ever spit.  Bring it On is also one of my favorite tracks on the album.  This track features Jaz-O and Sauce Money.  Regrets is a great track, Jay shows a little emotion on this one.  He also shows some love for his mother.  Can I Live II is a hot track.  Jay rips the verse but the original Can I Live still comes off better.Overall if you don't have Reasonable Doubt then you must not love hip hop.  This is one of the best albums of the 90s and anyone who claims to love rap music must have it.  It's one of those few albums that you can listen to from start to finish and not have to skip a track.  If you want quality music then you must have Reasonable Doubt.  I know that die hard Nas fans won't agree with this but this album is better than Illmatic for the simple fact that it has more tracks.  Illmatic was hot from start to finish and this was too, except longer.  This is one of those albums that never get old and can survive the test of time.  This album is this reason why Jay-Z has the right to be king of New York after Biggie died.  With the extremely inflated prices of cds today, this is one that is definitely worth the money.  No weak or average tracks to be found on this one.
summary: One of the best hip-hop albums of all time.  Perfection

reviewText: I feared the worst with this CD.  I found Alice's previous album, Eyes of Alice Cooper, good, not great.  When reading reports that this album kept to that sound I lowered my expectations a bit.  Once I got used to the "stripped down" garage style, which is more evident here than on Eyes, I started to really enjoy this disc.  Alice's wit, sneer, and sarcasm are all evident.  Most songs are catchy and made me drive 20 MPH faster than I should (that was the fault of "Run Down the Devil" and "Your Own Worst Enemy").  And hey, I even liked the rap song.I'll compare this one to Lace and Whiskey, with the diversity of songs and low production value.  That's a good thing.  Too much polish wouldn't help what he tried to achieve here, but two garage albums is just enough.
summary: I doubted the master, for that I bow in shame.

reviewText: While all of the preppy kids were jamming to "Loser," Beck released two more CD's almost simultaneously with MELLOW GOLD.  One was STEREOPATHETIC SOUL MANURE (see reviews), the other was this compilation of folk tracks, mis-titled, ONE FOOT IN THE GRAVE.  Excluding "Burnt Orange Peel," this is a CD full of songs right out of a Southern Baptist hymnal.  The music, almost entirely acoustic, is tradtitional as can be, and the lyrics are stellar.  The warped thing is how Beck weaves his modern day dimentia into these neoclassical hymns ("There's blood on the futon...there's a kid drinking fire."), and how he projects his own dismal outlook on our preppy society ("I got a funny feeling they got plastic in the afterlife"), yet, the songs still will fool your grandmother.  Quite a few of the tunes consist of Beck, by himself, with an acoustic guitar, and no digital effects or overdubs.  Songs like "Hollow Log" are crafted so beautifully, as though they could be played on ANY instrument and still sound good.  By no means were these guys just screwing around in the studio...there are too many gems on this CD, and too much talent (fellow Texan Chris Ballew of "The Pres. of the USA" accompanies on many of the tunes).  This CD can turn any hard rocker into an avid folk listener...the songs are too genuine to ignore.  TRY THIS--listen to this CD in an old pick-up truck with no AC driving through Oklahoma, Kansas or Nebraska, and tell me the Spirit doesn't move you...

reviewText: Even though Meatloaf has released about ten studio albums, only this one and its predecessor could be described as commerically "very successful." My theory is that people really LOVE Meatloaf...but only when they're sure he's about to give them what they want. And what they obviously want are the bombastic songs that are helmed under the _Bat Out of Hell_ name._Bat Out of Hell II_ is full of the typical Steinman songwriting--grand and extended song structures, passionate lyrical cliches, double entendrees and crescendos, and walls of vocals. Most know "I Would Do Anything For Love (But I Won't Do That)," and it holds up today as well as it did in '93. Other standout tracks are "Life Is a Lemon," "Rock and Roll Dreams Come Through," "It Just Won't Quit," and "Objects in the Rearview Mirror May Appear Closer than They Are." Heavier songs like "Wasted Youth" and "Out of the Frying Pan" are good, but the truly moving moments on the album is when Meatloaf is delivering his earnest and passionate vocals--he's truly in fine form on this album. "Objects in the Rearview Mirror," written by Steinman but semi-autobiographical of Meatloaf's own life, is a beautiful and powerful song. Cynics might laugh at the notion, and sometimes I myself even consider Meatloaf to be a "guilty pleasure," but you can't deny that this particular hybrid of rock-n-roll (part pop, part progressive rock, part heavy metal) is done extremely well.There's been rumors of _Bat Out of Hell III_ out there for quite some time, and if Steinman and Meatloaf are alive and well as this decade closes down, I'm sure we'll see it. In the meantime, pick up this album, sit back, and enjoy the wait.

Other standout tracks are "Life Is a Lemon," "Rock and Roll Dreams Come Through," "It Just Won't Quit," and "Objects in the Rearview Mirror May Appear Closer than They Are." Heavier songs like "Wasted Youth" and "Out of the Frying Pan" are good, but the truly moving moments on the album is when Meatloaf is delivering his earnest and passionate vocals--he's truly in fine form on this album. "Objects in the Rearview Mirror," written by Steinman but semi-autobiographical of Meatloaf's own life, is a beautiful and powerful song. Cynics might laugh at the notion, and sometimes I myself even consider Meatloaf to be a "guilty pleasure," but you can't deny that this particular hybrid of rock-n-roll (part pop, part progressive rock, part heavy metal) is done extremely well.There's been rumors of _Bat Out of Hell III_ out there for quite some time, and if Steinman and Meatloaf are alive and well as this decade closes down, I'm sure we'll see it. In the meantime, pick up this album, sit back, and enjoy the wait.

Very little style and half written in yellow letters. Even with my best reading glasses it requires great effort to decipher the text.

reviewText: Nobody exploits controversy quite like record labels so it's no surprise that after being sentenced to a ten-year bid for his part in the infamous 1999 club shooting that also involved mega-celebrities Sean "P. Diddy" Combs and Jennifer Lopez, that Jamal "Shyne" Barrow would become one of the most sought-after free agents in the game. Just a handful of weeks after inking a deal with Def Jam, the label quickly pushed out this thirteen-track collection of material that Shyne recorded before his incarceration.More than a few big names have shown up to help out Shyne on "Godfather Buried Alive". Kanye West contributes the production on "More Or Less", Ashanti and the Murder Inc. family bless "Jimmy Choo", and Foxy Brown backs up Po on "Tha Gang". Still, Shyne seems to put out his best work when he's the solo attraction as is the case on "Quasi O.G." and the dark but effective "Martyr", which is in my opinion the best track that Shyne has recorded so far. What is less impressive is "For The Record", a diss record towards 50 Cent that Shyne recorded over the telephone. Even with a beat behind it, the recording still sounds sloppy and hard to hear. It's too bad that for the first and only new track he has released since being locked up, he chose to go this route. Of the remaining songs, two have already been released, "Shyne", a year-old party track produced for Swizz Beat's 2002 compilation and the remix of "Behind The Walls", a four-year-old single from the Oz soundtrack. Both of them aren't bad by any means but may have worked better if they hadn't already been released for such a lengthy period of time.Some critics have attempted to compare "Buried Alive" to Pac's "Me Against The World", based solely on the similiar circumstances of their releases. Unfortunately that is really the only reason for the comparison. Shyne's second LP offers very little improvement over his self-titled debut. The production is solid but Shyne still seems caught up in his rhymes about guns and coke-dealing. Perhaps the fact that he had to rush to record a lot of his material before he got locked up has something to do with it but I still feel Shyne is capable of better.
