reviewText: Chet Baker had a voice that was very easy on the ear; and that voice of his also had just a touch of vulnerability to make it very special to his adoring audiences. Chet sings some very good numbers on this album and that's grand. Russ Freeman's musicians don't let us down, either! The quality of the sound is excellent and I really like that artwork, too."That Old Feeling" has Chet singing rather sweetly; he delivers this with panache and I'm impressed. "That Old Feeling" gets a rather jazzy arrangement and it works very well for Chet's rendition of this ballad. I always liked "That Old Feeling;" and Chet makes it sound very fresh and new. Great! "Like Someone In Love" gets a very sensitive treatment from Chet who sings this to perfection and beyond! Chet never sings a superfluous note; and the piano arrangement is very elegant as well. "My Ideal" uses the percussion very nicely; and Chet delivers this well. Chet handles complex key and tempo changes like the pro he always was--and he's right there front and center, too."I've Never Been In Love Before" is yet another most romantic tune that Chet infuses with great emotion as he wears his heart on his sleeve; and I really like "My Buddy." How's about that horn solo? In addition, "But Not For Me" shines bright; Chet swings gently to make this number a standout on the album and I could never tire of hearing Chet perform "But Not For Me.""I Get Along Without You Very Well (Except Sometimes)" is a very tender ballad; that xylophone works well and Chet sings this faultlessly. Chet uses that vulnerability in his voice to really make his performance all the better. Of course, "My Funny Valentine" is a major highlight of this album; Chet delivers this as only a true master ever could. Chet's incredible sense of timing amazes me and the gentle music that goes along fits in perfectly with Chet's vocals."The Thrill Is Gone" has Chet Baker squarely front and center--right where he belongs! I really like "The Thrill Is Gone;" Chet performs this wonderfully and that horn makes the music very beautiful. "I Fall In Love Too Easily" shines brighter than silver and gold when Chet sings it; and the album ends very well with Chet Baker performing a very classic pop vocal entitled "Look For The Silver Lining." "Look For The Silver Lining" gets an upbeat melody and the tempo is just right for this ballad. Chet aces this last tune as effortlessly as if it were just breathing. Of course, it really wasn't that easy; but Chet's talents always carried him through.Chet Baker fans will want this CD; it really highlights his fine talents as a singer in particular. This is also a great starter CD for people just discovering the artistry of the great Chet Baker.
summary: Chet could sell a song without even trying--BRAVO, CHET BAKER !!!

reviewText: "Surfacing" is one of the most beautiful albums in Sarah McLachlan's career.  This is less rock themed than her previous album "Falling Toward Ectasy".  She sings her every drop of heart and soul through every track.  Her every track has heavy emotion that slams the listeners in a good way.  The spiritual "Angel" symbolizes this the most.  Her songwriting is amazing.  Every instrument combines with her beautiful soprano voice wonderfully, even the edgy electric guitar parts most expressed on "Witness" and "Black And White".  Such combination heard on every track remains unique and ahead of its time.  McLachlan plays the guitar and the piano as soulfully as she sings.  She proves on "Surfacing" that she continues to evolve as a musician.  Such high level talent will give her legendary status in the following years to come.  This album is great for those looking for something unique and relaxing.  Many will be pleased.

reviewText: This is my all-time favorite VU album. "What Goes On" is one of the best, most underrated pure jamming rock songs ever recorded.The album has a mellow intensity. What I think of as the triad of "Jesus", "I'm Beginning to See the Light", and "I'm Set Free" is spiritually uplifting without being silly or sappy or corny.Most importantly, this album is what the Velvet Underground was all about. Just imagine one year purchasing the dissonant noise of White Light/White Heat, then putting on this album. They were always one step ahead of their audience, a group measured in thousands, not millions. While their counterparts were dropping acid, picking up sitars and following charlatan prophets, VU was pushing the boundaries of rock and roll, blowing minds with screeching machine sounds and screaming violins, and melding avante garde classical with Brill Building pop to produce unforgettable "classic" songs about S&M, Heroin, transvestites (Candy Says, on this album) and Jesus.But then again, they were from the Lower East Side of Manhattan, not West Hollywood or Marin County. Things looked different from down there.

reviewText: I enjoy the music on this CD.  It is a finely crafted performance.  Tom Morello creates a compelling aural landscape, exploring the outter reaches of guitar sound.  TESTIFY, CALM LIKE A BOMB, and ASHES IN THE FALL each feature a glissando which is controlled chaos that could slip away from less nimble fingers.  My favourite songs are those which have RATM in a solid funk groove, as on CLAB, BORN OF A BROKEN MAN and NEW MILLENNIUM HOMES.  This heavy construction aggro-hip-hop provides the perfect platform for Zack's precisely, punctuated, politically powered, philippic poetry.  RATM are an easy target for jaded criticism which suggests they sing songs about other peoples' problems.  A quick glance at the luxury cars in the parking lots of their concerts betrays the "rebel" facade of their audiences.  It may be posing, but it's not vapid, and the band is sincere.  Zack and crew fuel "tha fire only [Bob] Marley could catch". Even if their audience has never been oppressed, they are shown how to put their affluence to support those less fortunate.  On the last page of the notes are listed nearly a dozen organizations who fight for the rights of those about whom RATM sings.  If you are interested in aggro-hip-hop heavy metal with politically motivated lyrics, this CD will interest you.  Even if you don't, you may be interested in helping the organizations which can benefit from your support. Peace.

reviewText: My bias lies in the love of a singer and a guitar.  I love performers doing solo work, and this is about as stripped down as you can get.  This was a sort of comeback breakthrough thing for the man in black, and a stunning work it is.  I appreciate it all, from the salvation to the murder, as it is a multifaceted view of Cash.  I am a bit put of by the live recordings, just because it smacks of hipster audiences.  They cheer at yell at the most ridiculous things.  This however is not Johnny's fault.  He has the greatest ability to turn any piece into something that becomes completely his.  Take the GLenn Danzig song  Thirteen.  This is a true Cash experience, haunting, broody...  and then he turns around and does a religious tune, one about vietnam, and closes with the satiric Man who Couldn't cry.  This is a beautiful work.  I wholeheartedly recommend it.

reviewText: Ok, let me get a couple of things straight from the outset. Im a huge Pearl Jam fan, and I didnt buy this album expecting, or wanting, to hear 'Ten' part two. In that respect, I wasnt disappointed. This certainly isnt a rehash of anything theyve ever done before: Pearl Jam cosistently branch out into new musical directions without sacrificing their artistc integrity or failing to showcase the remerkable talents of each and every band member that got us all interested in the first place. Sadly though, this certainly isnt Pearl Jam's best album. Its not their best since 'Ten', or their best since 'Vs', or better than 'Vitalogy' or 'No code'. Dont get me wrong, its not their worst either: it has wonderful moments. But let me tackle this in detail.I was struck at first by the way the albums two opening tracks act as a kind of simulacrum of the No Code formula. A slow opener, building into a racuous, full throttle rocker for the second track. Its a formula that worked perfectly in 1996: sadly, 'Cant Keep' and 'Save you' just arent anywhere near as good as 'Sometimes' and 'Hail hail', precipitating unwelcome comparisons. Despite this, 'Save You' is a great track, and the albums only real straightahead rocker. After all this negativity, now would be a good time to bestow some praise on one man: Matt Cameron. He contributes more to this album than Binaural, and im massively impressed. Many people forget he penned some of the best Soundgarden tunes, and hes well up to standard here. 'You are' is my favourite track here: a truly stunning song which takes Pearl Jam into uncharted waters, a really strange song that Ive fallen in love with irrevocably. Thanks to this Id honestly say its worth buying the album just for that track. Unfortunately one great track doesnt make a wonderful album. What we have here is a good album. 'Cropduster' and 'get right', camerons other compositions, are superb, 'I am mine' really is great, as is the folky 'thumbing my way', which once again shows us just what a diverese, talented songsmith Vedder is. Elsewhere, half full, and all or none provide other highlights. Its a good album, but i cant help feeling if it had all been up to the standards of you are or I am mine, it could have been their best. Still worth buying, even for the casual fan. Pearl jam continue to evolve and immpress, but theres an essential fire that has gone.
summary: Im glad I gave it a chance.

Its a good album, but i cant help feeling if it had all been up to the standards of you are or I am mine, it could have been their best. Still worth buying, even for the casual fan. Pearl jam continue to evolve and immpress, but theres an essential fire that has gone.

reviewText: You know the feeling - It's the first day of spring, birds are singing, flowers are blooming, it's about 75 degrees out, and the smell of freshly-cut grass is in the air.  It's been so long since the weather was this nice (at least in the Midwest) - that's what I like to compare this album to.  It's fresh, it's got personality, and it's really easy to listen to.I admit, this is my first Ivy purchase, though I've heard all their albums at one time or another.  This is my favorite, and the most accessible, for those who are looking to start listening to Ivy.One of my personal favorites is "Thinking About You", with its blissful, so-happy-you-want-to-slap-someone vocals and driving rhythm.  It's almost TOO cutesy, but it'll perk you up."Keep Moving" is another favorite, with it's disco-esque beat, funky guitars in the back, and bumping bassline, I think this song would be really complete with one of those fruity disco flutes tooting away in the back somewhere. Dominique skips across the beat flawlessly on this one, and even when the lyrics aren't quite so happy ("All I can do / in a world without you / is keep moving"), she sounds like she's still bouncing around."Tess Don't Tell" is similar to "Thinking About You" in format, fast beat, husky vocals, guitars, but for some reason, it's completely different.  Fresh - just like this album, when you compare it to the excess fluff in the pop scene these days.  Free your mind - this is what good music sounds like.  And sure, if you're my age, you might get all sorts of homosexuality-themed remarks thrown your way in traffic when you turn this up in your car, but that's all the more incentive to turn it up more and drown out whatever their bandwagon's playing at the moment.

reviewText: If anyone's worried Interview is the first step in the wrong direction for Gentle Giant, fear not, because besides a couple questionable moments that are overlong and repeat a bit much, this is definitely a quality album on the same level as the previous GG albums.The odd time signatures, the vocal melodies that repeat a lot, but are quite catchy... all the things you love about the band have remained in check with Interview.  I sense the band was starting to feel worn out by this time in their career, which is indicated by the lyrics in a few of the songs, such as "Another Show".  My favorite song is "I Lost My Head".  Extremely good vocal melodies here.There's one song on here that has a tropical vibe with lyrics about money (how appropriate with todays economy!)  I'm amazed the lead singers voice is still in incredibly good shape- he hasn't lost a step since the previous album.  This is just great rock and roll that's played in a complex, yet very satisfying way.

reviewText: ("Octahedron" by The Mars Volta)This is easily the most straightforward album of the Mars Volta's career.  None of the songs are longer than 8:22 (album closer "Luciforms")--amazing concisement on their part, and a couple of the songs here could pass as--gasp!--ballads ("Since We've Been Wrong,", "With Twilight as My Guide"). Hell, most of the songs even have recognizable melodies, with choruses and everything!  Could this be the Volta's "commercial sellout" album?Well, hold on, buddy.  You can't just accuse the Mars Volta--the most willfully surreal prog-rock band out there--of just wanting to sell records.  Okay, I have no idea what kind of numbers some of their previous discs have racked up, but but with long, twisty compositions that often bleed into each other and musical digressions that often go into jazz fusion, latin rhythms and liberal doses of synthed-out spaciness, one doubts the band is on speking terms with the editors of Billboard, never mind the low-attention span record buying public.  Nevertheless, the band has maintained a healthy cult following.  Still, "Octahedron" definitely shows signs of warming up to the marketplace.You know what?  It turns out that's not a bad thing.  "Octahedron" is indeed shorter and, yes, softer, than any of the band's previous albums, but it's also one of the most memorable.  Not only are the band technically great musicians, but they can also write songs that stick with you.  "Teflon," for instance, is one of their best rockers, mainly because they manage to color within the lines.  Omar Rodriguez-Lopez's lyrics still are plenty loopy--"Frames of infrared/keep scrolling into focus/Scarab claimed the busy signal/With the habits that you noticed"--but really, that's one of the reasons people love them.Does this new direction mean that even more people will come to love them as well?  I couldn't tell you that.  Heck, "Octahedron" is hardly even my fave Volta disc (I swear byFrances the Mute, still the band's most out-there album), but I get the feeling this on'll keep me coming back for more.  It should also be noted that when I say this album is "more" commercial than previous material, that shoudn't be confused with, uh, "commercial."  The band are still a pretty daunting listen, and it's still very easy to tell them apart from the current crop of "popular" rock bands, so I don't think the cultists will have to make much room for the uncool just yet.

reviewText: I had not listened to the album as a whole for some time, having reheard it a couple of time recently, I concluded that it was not quite as good as In remembered it to be, though still a great and very listenable album that really is the one where Cohen begins his journey towards the rock approach that would give us “I’m Your Man” and “The Future”.Though the basics for “New Skin For Old Ceremony” are still Cohen’s acoustic guitar and his voice, he is here incorporating different styles and uses a broader musical palette.The album has its stand-out moments with “Chelsea Hotel #2”- which is one of Cohen’s greatest songs ever and one of the most covered, I believe – I think Lloyd Cole’s version is great and really catchy.“Who By the Fire” is catchy as it is – great and differently arranged showing Cohen going in new and broader directions than on his first albums, which were pretty simply and sparsely arranged.“Take this Longing” is “old” Cohen style, and another of his great songs.

reviewText: I first learned of Ras Kass through 2 hip-hop magazines, XXL and the Source. I then downloaded a few of his songs and decided to purchase his CD, proof that downloadable music is a good promotional tool. This CD is probably the best balance between underground and commercial tracks. "Ghetto Fabulous" featuring Mack 10 and Dr. Dre should've been made into a single, but unfortunately Ras Kass' record label holds him back. The producer of several of the tracks, including "Ghetto Fabulous" and "Rasassination", Stu-B-Doo, is where Ras Kass made his mistake- he should've used him more. Ras Kass' new album should be out soon, but it will likely not be able to compare to Rasassination, and his earlier release, Soul On Ice, didn't have the beats to compare to this bangin' album. If you like Hip-Hop music in general, this album has it all-gangsta beats (Ghetto Fabulous), underground tracks (Rassasination), a track for the Wu-Tang obsessed, (The End featuring The RZA), concept songs (Interview With A Vampire featuring God and Satan) and thoughtful lyricism (every track!). So whether you love West Coast Rap, East Coast Rap, intense lyricism, underground rap, commercial rap, or phat beats, you should get your own copy of Rasassination. I also recommend Soul On Ice, but don't think Ras can obtain perfection more than once.
summary: Ras Kass, The Illest MC Of All Time

reviewText: I first became aware of Grace Potter and the Nocturnals when they performed at an event for my company last summer.  I liked what I heard, and I gave their eponymous album a try.  From what I understand it was a departure from their previous work, and The Lion The Beast The Beat is a continuation of their musical evolution.  While Potter has a more dynamic voice, this album reminds me of Sheryl Crow's Globe Sessions (which I still consider to be her best) in the style of music.  I think that they captured the essence of what made that album great without sounding derivative.That being said let's get specific about the songs.  For starters the opener/title track is interesting in many ways.  The song is structured in three parts that have slightly different feels.  It opens sparsely with understated vocals "I found the heart of a lion in the belly of the beast.  And I held it in my hand and I could feel.  I could feel, feel the beat."  A tempo change follows as the "beat" is called forth.  In the chorus Potter tells us that "Life is a record playing on repeat."  The final section of the song starts over the final minute or so with violin flourishes layered in.  Potter's vocal delivery is spot on, and this song sets a high bar for the remainder of the album.The theme that runs through The Lion The Beast The Beat is one of loss, sorrow, and sadness.  It's in the vocals "Timekeeper" - "I'm too young to be feeling this way", "Loneliest Soul" - "I'm the loneliest soul so leave me alone.", and "One Heart Missing" - "If love is made for two, there's one heart missing".  Also "Stars" is one of the true ballads on the album, and it features a mournful guitar solo.  Finally there is the blues rock song "Runaway" in which Potter simply asks "...let me go..."I mentioned The Globe Sessions at the beginning, and the clearest nod on The Lion The Beast The Beat is "Never Go Back".  The opening beat calls to mind "There Goes The Neighborhood" in a strong way.  I also found a similarity to perhaps a less known band - Elizabeth and the Catapult.  The piano opening of "Timekeeper" reminds me a lot of "Time (We All Fall Down)" from The Other Side of Zero (see my review).Overall, I think that The Lion The Beast The Beat is a great album, and I would recommend it to anyone who likes blues rock featuring very talented female singers.Download this:  The Lion The Beast The Beat

(Later to be sampled by Dr. Dre in his song, "Let Me Ride.")  All of the songs are on a whole different level from other records.  Everyone knows the classic "Tear the Roof Off the Sucka," but I think that the last song, "Night of the Thumpasorus Peoples" is by far the funkiest. If you buy it and think it wasnt worth your money, then you dont have a pulse, because this is straight funk.  Also buy the lp's that I noted on above, "One Nation ..." and "Funkentelechy..."  George and the boys get way less credit than they deserve, because if it werent for him, rap and some of the modern rock wouldn't be here today, not to mention not having the great songs to dance to that they created.  5 stars outta 5. reviewText: Fusioned by a combination of classic balladry, soul, and alternative/techno music, "Bedtime Stories" is one of Madonna's best albums to date. As the years progressed, Madonna became much more mature in her musical styles, and after all the hoopla from the controversy her "Sex" book caused, she decided to take a much more modest approach with this album. While I'm not saying that her "Erotica" album was bad, because in reality it was one of her best, "Bedtime Stories" allowed Madonna to venture into new musical territory and producers.Produced by musical powerhouse producer Babyface, "Bedtime Stories" opens up with "Survival," which has Madonna recounting that while she wasn't totally a saint on her way to the top, her success was a survival story. She's right (critics penned her as a one-hit wonder and predicted Cyndi Lauper as the next big thing during the 1980's) and this song is a great opener for a great album."Secret" and "Human Nature" have their share of funk, and provide the listener with enough dance/club music to keep their interest in this album satisfied. However most of the album reflects Madonna's journey into the world of ballads and soft-pop that has garnered her many new fans lately."Take a Bow" and "Forbidden Love" captured Madonna's magic in using her vocals in producing an effective approach when singing slow, love songs. "Inside of Me" is a sensual, slow, and soft song that speaks of Madonna's longing for love (not necessarily sexual, but the song does emit that to the listener) inside of her.However, my two favorite songs on this album have to be "Love Tried To Welcome Me" and "Bedtime Story." On the former, we get to hear Madonna's vocals amidst a blend of string instruments and a Spanish-style guitar, talking about rejected love. The song is mesmerizing in every sense of the word, and this Babyface produced track has to be the best ballad on this album."Bedtime Story", which marks Madonna's first journey into the world of alternative music, was written by Bjork, the reigning queen of alternative rock, and produced by Nellee Hooper (of "Soul II Soul" fame). The sound of this song, its' effects, and even the companion music video (the second most-expensive music video in history, and a mind tripping work of art; it's available on her "93:99" video collection) blew me away then and now, and it is one of my favorite techno tracks ever.If you haven't already purchased this album, please do so! Madonna is truly a pioneer in whatever she does, and this album happens to be one of her best in recent years.

reviewText: To say that ''Protection'' was Massive Attack's worst album is being incoherently unfair, it is equally good as their previous and subsequent work.I like ''Mezzanine'', ''Blue Lines'' and ''100th Window'' but ''Protection'' is one of my ultimate favores...most likely because Tracy Thorn teamed up with them on two of the cuts (which were both releases). The title track ''Protection'' is definitely Massive Attack's best cut ever (vocally)....It's a pity that Tracy Thorn was only a guest vocalist then, its a real shame that she hasn't teamed up with them again.Massive Attack would do much better if they'd invite in- much more talented vocalists. For example; Tracy Thorn, Nicollette, Madonna and Bjork are arguably the best vocalists Massive Attack has ever teamed up with, of course in Madonna's case, they only teamed up with her once in 1996 in for the restructure of ''I Want You'' which was commercially released on the ''Something To Remember'' album and peaked a healthy 14# In the top 40 Charts.In tracks like ''Sly'' you have the smoky and pining vocals of Nicollette which are just as captivating as Tracy Thorn's and Tricky's vocals. ''Weather Storms'' carries out possibly the best musical tune throughout this label, ''Spying Glass'' features rare fragments of Horace Andy. ''Better Things'' which carries out thin sharp and glass-breaking sound effects with a very much light beat, to me this track is the most accessible cut from this album with lyrics like ''Don't Drag me down, Just Because you're down'', in addition to that you have Tracy Thorn's voice which reaches its highest peak...definitely able to send chills down your spine and keep your finger at the repeat button...The only disappointment is that the track is short.The other tracks are ok, I didn't like the live version of ''Light My Fire''. This LP may be the most unusual album of Massive Attack......but that doesn't make it a bad album...on the contrary its one of their best, seeing its more humane and less involved than ''Mezzanine'' was...In ''Mezzanine'' there was too much of everything, and too much can always end up insolvent.

reviewText: "Souvenirs" is one of Dan Fogelberg's strongest works. This is a fairly eclectic collection.You can find a song for almost every mood here. There's the sparkling upbeat opener "Part of the Plan" which received most of the airplay from this collection. "Someone's Been Telling You Stories" rolls out in a smoky tempo taking the part of a man who's been lied about. "Song from Half Mountain" is just Dan singing with his guitar, telling the story of a beautiful part of nature in such a personal way that he could almost be in your living room.There's really no bad Dan Fogelberg and I've said that before his untimely death. I'd neglected to upgrade "Souvenirs" from vinyl and I'm very glad I did.Rebecca Kyle, June 2008

reviewText: It amazes me that the themes and sentiments that Marvin Gaye expressed in 1972 are still so contentious and relevant in the age of this 'new millenium'.  Racism, taxes, war, poverty, jobs, pollution, drug usage, etc...  And in the 30 years since it was originally released it would appear that very little has changed.This album is more like a collection of related short stories than a musical work.  It always amazes me how smoothly the transitions occur between songs that have different themes, tempos, and sentiments.  You're totally unaware of when one song ends and another begins.The instruments range from bongos to violins.  And all are seemlessly interwoven to paint the pictures of desperation, pain, disbelief, confusion, outrage, friendship, love, and mercy.This would probably be one of the 5 albums that I would want to take to a deserted island if I had to go.
summary: An urban opera (or opus) from an R&B maestro

reviewText: When Liars hit the music scene in 2001, the name of their album and song titles weren't the only thing that seemed a little peculiar to everyone.  This was a band that had chewed up the mass of their influences and spit them out in an entirely new fashion.  With only one record, they created a buzz that even they couldn't get rid of if they wanted to.  Upon arrival of their unique debut release, They Threw Us All in a Trench and Stuck a Monument on Top, critics and fans alike were fast to realize Liars was stylistically similar to a lot of the other NYC-based bands revitalizing the late 70's/early 80's post-punk dance scene.  Even so, while they were immediately pigeonholed into this category, they were able to add an edgy, almost avant-garde, boldness that the others were simply not exploring.The same can also be said for They Were Wrong, So We Drowned.  The only thing here that's similar to their debut is that the song titles and album name are still very unique (both albums start with the word `they').  With that aside, the primary thing you'll discover once you listen to this album is that things have drastically changed - for the better.  The envelope has been moved in an entirely new direction, and the band wouldn't have it any other way.  Liars take great pride in breaking out of the genre-defining boxes they're thrown in.  In the same way Radiohead took an impeccable album like OK Computer and stepped into unfamiliar territory with Kid A, Liars have sidestepped the majority of their familiar styles and broken free towards new explorations.  Now, I won't go so far as to say They Were Wrong sounds like Kid A, but it definitely gives me the same feelings I had the first time I heard that album.There's a detached coldness that emanates in They Were Wrong.  Perhaps it's due to the fact that a type of German witchcraft, known as Walpurgisnacht, inspired the album.  Whatever the reason, the album is very dense, imaginative, and executed with chaotic precision.  "Broken Witch" begins with disconnected electronics and a drum machine that has you immediately finding this record more electronic than it's predecessors.  In many cases, the drums have been played live, recorded, and then manipulated to assist in this concept.  "There's Always Room on the Broom" is a distorted beauty with its heavy microphone feedback and high-pitched vocals.  The best track, "We Fenced Other Houses with the Bones of Our Own," is easily the most sinuous moment of the album, and simply impossible not to compare to the same approach Radiohead took on Kid A.  The instrumental "Read the Book That Wrote Itself" is a collection of eerie keyboard sounds with ritualistic drumming and pencil writing.  As with They Threw Us All In a Trench, the longest song,  "Flow My Tears the Spider Said" is saved until the end of the album.  Although I really tried to stay away from this comparison, I can't help but think it's strikingly similar in some ways to The Beatles "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds."  It's then slowly faded away to the sounds of birds and minimal instrumentation.They Were Wrong, So We Drowned is an incredibly tight album, and it's surely going to be one of the year's first greatly admired albums.  Each song is independent to the others, yet collectively this album is very cohesive.  Since the songs all bare similarities in visual terms, I guess you could say it's a concept album of sorts.  If breaking free from their own mold is this band's forte, then I imagine we are going to hear quite an array of sounds in future releases.  One thing you'll always be assured of is that Liars show up to give a great and lasting impression whenever they enter the studio.  They prove once again that even with their rotation of musicians, they are capable of taking the scene by the hair and utilizing their talents in every way possible to remain one of the most exciting bands around.

reviewText: Alanis Morissette's most under-rated masterpiece, Supposed Former Infatuation Junkie is her finest and complex work. A very moody album, very saracastic, cynical, but does have moments have passion and self-awarness. Alanis is one brainy woman, her lyrics are incredible, top-notch and cool. Standout tracks include: Front Row, Joining You, I was Hoping, U R, Can't Not, Would Not Come, Are you still Mad?, Unsent, and So Pure. Alanis didn't even want to record another record after the huge success of Jagged Little Pill, her success over-whelmed her and left the songtress empty and exhausted from supporting and touring with the album. Producer Glen Ballard and her friends finally convinced Alanis to record again and ever since that moment she has never stopped creating positive and great music. A perfect album, 17 tracks, boy that's a lot. Hear this album when you're feeling down, it will make you feel more alive and human afterwords. Powerful words from a powerful woman, Alanis rocks!

reviewText: When looking at Olivia Newton-John's career, one must look at it from the perspective of her as a vocalist.  You aren't going to find a lot of songs where Olivia is going to be the songwriter - and you aren't going to find her playing a lot of instruments.  Olivia does what she does best - provide some outstanding vocals.  Therefore, Olivia is going to have a strong reliance on good songwriting and good supporting musicians.  What a lot of people probably don't remember is that when Olivia started out as a vocalist in the 1970s, she came up through the Country and Folk Music ranks.  Olivia's crossover into a mainstream/pop artist would coincide with her film debut in the movie-version of "Grease".  That film would establish her as a Superstar.  However as fast as Olivia's Star rose, she would fall into oblivion by the end of the 1980s.  However, Olivia's successful career has resulted in some nice collections of her vocal work.  One such collection is "Olivia Newton-John: Back to Basics - The Essential Collection 1971-1992".  It serves as a reverse chronology of Olivia's work starting with 1992 and going back to her early days as a Country artist.There are two things that set "Back to Basics" apart from many of the other Olivia Newton-John compilations that are available today.  For starters, it contains four new recordings that are unavailable on any of the other greatest hits sets.  The other thing is that this compilation goes in reverse chronological order.  Normally I prefer my Greatest Hits collections to have the tracks arranged in chronological order. This allows me to see how the artist has progressed and evolved over time. "Back to Basics" does the reverse.  While I still would have liked to have seen this in regular chronological order, I found the reverse order to be an interesting twist.  It fits very nicely with the title "Back to Basics"."Back to Basics" isn't the most complete collection out there.  While it does contain some nice songs, there are some very good Olivia songs that are missing.  The songs I would have liked to have seen included are: "Don't Stop Believin",  "Let it Shine", "He Ain't Heavy He's My Brother", "Come on Over",  "Take Me Home Country Roads", "Me and Bobby McGee", "Don't Cry for me Argentina", "Heart Attack", and "Make a Move on Me"As mentioned, there are several other Compilations out there.  The following lists some of the more popular compilations.  Here are some important notes when looking at these compilations:"Greatest Hits": This collection contains 12 songs covering all of the albums before "Grease".  The songs on "Back to Basics" that precede the "Grease" songs are all included on this collection""Greatest Hits 2": This collection contains 10 songs from "Grease" to "Physical".  While "Back to Basics" contains 7 songs from this period, "Greatest Hits 2" doesn't contain "Deeper Than the Night" or the duets with John Travolta - "You're the One that I Want" and "Summer Nights"."Magic - The Best of Olivia Newton-John":  This is a 21-song set that covers Olivia's career through 1983's "Twist of Fate" (the point where Olivia's career went into decline).  All of the songs on "Back to Basics" (with the exception of the four new tracks) are contained on this collection.  In addition, this collection contains the "Grease Mega Mix" that gained popularity a few years ago."The Best of Olivia Newton-John": This is a 18-song collection that goes deeper with Olivia's early work (i.e. early to mid 1970s songs).As mentioned while this is not the most complete collection, it does contain four new songs by Olivia.  I wouldn't do "handstands" for these new Olivia songs, but they aren't bad.  Olivia gets some help from some industry "names" for these songs:"Deeper than a River": This song was written and produced by Diane Warren. reviewText: Seals and Crofts is perhaps one of the 70s strangest success stories.  It's hard to categorize their music...sometimes pop; sometimes folk; often rock; and even jazz.  But always dynamic, melodic and memorable.  Without possessing glamour-boy looks, they crafted elegant songs, often invoking personal religious beliefs, which in the future would stall their careers (the wonderful UNBORN CHILD).At any rate, the duo's entire catalogue finally made it to CD, including SUMMER BREEZE.The hit title song invokes the joys of both summer and a happily married man.  The album's other hit, HUMMINGBIRD, utilizes soaring harmonies and haunting imagery to assimmilate the gentle hum of the titular bird.The joy of S&C;'s music is you never knew what to expect---the playful feel of FUNNY LITTLE MAN; the raw energy of YELLOW DIRT and SAY; the exuberance of FIDDLE IN THE SKY; the sheer beauty of EAST OF GINGER TREES, ADVANCE GUARDS and THE BOY DOWN THE ROAD.Their use of instruments like the dulcimer and mandolin gave them an identifiable sound not heard by the pop/rock audiences.SUMMER BREEZE is an extremely entertaining album, expertly helmed by Louie Shelton and excellently remastered.

reviewText: This might not have been the very first Gangsta Rap album, but with the rage in Ice Cube's voice and the premium production of Dr. Dre this is the album that set the stage for mainstream Gangsta Rap even without the help of radio or MTV.  An acronym for Niggaz With Attitude these guys packed all of the attitude of Compton into this disc.  With MC Ren and Ice Cube spitting in your face street lyrics like a p***ed off Chuck D anyone who heard this couldn't dodge the impact of the subject matter.  "F*** The Police", which of course warranted the imfamous letter from the F.B.I., was a dose of shocking realism at the time as was the rest of the album.  Eazy E adds the Flavor Flav quasi-comic relief making this an all around entertaining album.  DJ Yella assists Dre with the beats coming together with Bomb Squad's hardcore sonic influences and adding some West Coast flavor to them.  As noted at the beginning of this review N.W.A. were not the first Gangsta Rappers, but as is often the case in music it's the ones who perfect the genre that get the recognition rather than the innovators.  And perfect Gangsta Rap is exactly what N.W.A. does with STRAIGHT OUTTA COMPTON.

reviewText: travis' debut makes no bones about its intent to be a trad-rock album.  maybe the best way to describe it is a 90s version of what the beatles would probably sound like if they recorded today.  straightaway, loud guitar music thrives here, on the anthemic "all i wanna do is rock," and the exasperated "tied to the 90s."  there is some real lyrical quality here, which you might not notice upon first listen.  "u16 girls" is quite a number with its unabashed love for yes, younger women, although its cautionary message is probably meant as more humorous and innocent than serious; "i love anyways" is not standard and predicatable as the title might imply ("i think you should be framed in some fine art gallery / i know you disagree with me" for example is charming and beautiful at the same time).  few tracks lag ("happy" is probably one of the weaker tunes, though outside of the chorus' lyrics it isn't so bad), as fran healy really can carry a song with his charisma, much more so than liam gallagher.  his voice is affable and endearing, whether it's in a subtle whisper or a borderline scream.  travis also manages to throw in a good amount of diversifying instrumentation, notably on "good feeling" and the wonderful closer "funny thing," which might be the album's best song.  however, other that the charm this album has, there is nothing to truly distinguish it musically from oasis and standard classicist brit-pop fare.  it's done masterfully, but it's not terribly innovative, though that's not to say it isn't enjoyable and worthwhile.  as many point out, "good feeling" is much more of a straight-up rock n roll album than its successor, the subdued and principally acoustic "the man who."  the albums complement each other and reveal a band that understands its roots and influences but isn't afraid to change things up, because repeating themselves is the last thing they want to do.

reviewText: This is an extremely unusual rendition of "Silent Night," performed on the acoustic guitar, and I must admit that I needed to listen to it six or seven times before it started to grow on me.  During the introduction, I thought John Fahey was attempting to play the song with a hint of a Hawaiian influence, but then the stylistic influences seemed to come into the song from a multitude of directions, almost to the point that the song seemed to lack cohesion in places.Do I want "Silent Night" played in this fashion?  Maybe not.  But I'll keep it around because it is fascinating to listen to the multitude of musical techniques he uses.  There is no doubt that Mr. Fahey was an extremely talented musician, and I enjoyed listening to the sheer artistry and creativity that went into recording the song.  I'm glad it was offered as a free download, so I’ll be generous and round it up my rating to four stars.

reviewText: Natalie is the floacist, Marsha is the songstress, and together they are Floetry.  Floetry has created a timeless masterpiece with their debut, "Floetic".  This CD is filled with well written songs, mostly about relationships and love.  The feel of the album is laid back; most of the songs are slow or mid tempo.  I would like to let potential buyers know that Floetry's image is kind of on the plain side, but after listening to their music, you will be swept away, I was!  It's safe to say that Floetry is "neo soul" like India.Arie, Erykah Badu, Angie Stone, Musiq and D'Angelo.  Neo soul is a term that means old music meets new music.Their first single is "Floetic", which is one of the only faster songs on the CD.  This is a nice song to dance to and was a nice way for these ladies to begin their career.  The song was a hit but it didn't catch the attention of music listeners like some debut songs do.  It wasn't until the second single, "Say Yes", that people began to show a genuine interest in Floetry.  This song received very heavy airplay and was well received by music listeners.  The song is very nice and shows a very mature Floetry, whereas "Floetic" showed Floetry on a more playful side.  "Getting Late" is the groups third single and by now the Floetry buzz is becoming quite heavy.  More and more people are beginning to buy the album because they have heard these three great singles.  They see the creative style of these women; Marsha, for the most part, lays the vocals down while Natalie adds her rap/spoken word.  "If I Was a Bird" is a very nice ballad.  This song has very nice lyrics and was produced well.  It's an album highlight because Marsha's vocals are especially strong on this cut.  "Ms Stress" is one of those songs that touches most women.  The woman in the song is a mistress and knows that it hurts being the woman on the side.  This is one of the best songs on the CD because not only do both women shine on this track, the words are so touching.  Floetry helped write Michael Jackson's "Butterflies", so as an added bonus, they included the demo version on the CD.  It sounds really good, just as good as Michael's version.  Floetry also did background vocals on MJ's version.I get something different from this CD after each listen.  I believe everyone who listens to it will get something from it.  ALL YOU GOTTA DO IS SAY YES!  5 STARS.Mikeisha's Top 51. Ms Stress2. Say Yes3. Getting Late4. Butterflies5. If I Was a Bird

reviewText: Just 2 years after the release of his classic sophomore album Eminem was ready to release another one.  After I listened to this album it's obvious that Eminem has changed his image big time, he doesn't rap about taking drugs, raping women or brutally killing people.  This is easily Eminem's most mature and complete effort yet.  It is arguably a borderline classic, but I'm going to say that it's just below one and still worth a 5 star rating.  At this point Eminem was really impressing many people across the world and went on to sell 8 million copies in the U.S.When the lead single, 'Without Me' was released, I was sort of impressed with it.  Once you hear the album you will realize that it's one of the weaker tracks but it's still good.  So that should really tell you that this album is definitely dope.  The skits aren't as good on this album.  The Paul skit was alright and the Steve Berman was real funny.  The intro is just a curtain raising and Eminem approaching the mic, the outro is the curtain falling with Ken Kaniff coming to the mic and rapping something gay..just changing around some words from the intro to 'Without Me.'  The production was real nice; Dr. Dre and Eminem doing all of it with a few co-producers.  My favorite beats have to be 'Soldier,' 'Say What You Say' and 'Till I Collapse.'  All the choruses are hot.  My favorite has to be 'Till I Collapse.'  The guest appearances include Dr. Dre, Obie Trice, D12 and Nate Dogg.  I was impressed with all of their parts, no weak links on the guest appearances which is always good.  No real fillers, you should enjoy every song except for the maybe the overplayed 'Without Me' and 'Cleanin Out My Closet.'  I would suggest this album to any rap fan.  Underground heads won't like this though.  It's worth your money so go out and buy it to support the most successful rap artist of all time.

reviewText: This difference between this album and all the others is that it actually contains some really bad songs. If you were to take the best songs from every Eagles album and compare them, only Hotel California would be stronger than The Long Run. But of course, there are 10 songs on the album. I Can't Tell You Why and Heartache Tonight are the best songs on the album. Schmitt did a helluva a job replacing Randy Meisner. His bass, vocals and vocal harmony are every bit as good as Meisner's. The Sad Cafe, In The City and the title track are all also excellent songs. The King of Hollywood is a dark and good song, but it is no Hotel California, for sure. The rest is crap. The Disco Strangler is the worst Eagles song by a mile and the only Teenage Jail even rates "filler" status. Still, this is a very enjoyable album, even if it is probably the worst single their debut album.

reviewText: To have such a collection from Jimi after 30 + years is a real treat.  It's such a tease to hear this music and think of what more there might have been.  Jimi and bandmates Billy Cox and Mitch Mitchell delve deeply into a funk-rock sound, leaving behind the psychedelia that was a mainstay of Jimi's first three studio albums.  The mood of the music is upbeat, and the lyrics are consistently interesting, and generously laced with Hendrix humor.  The arrangements are densely packed, yet lively and loose - a credit to Hendrix's own production.  Standout tracks are "Freedom", "Dolly Dagger", "Ezy Rider", "Drifting" and "My Friend", and each of these belongs in the pantheon of great Hendrix performances.  And for anyone who wonders what Jimi's state of mind was in the period immediately preceding his death, I get the sense from this album that he was a happy man, feeling at the top of his game and looking intensely into the future.Drawbacks?  Well, yes, although with Hendrix's untimely death during the creation of this album, we have to assume that some of the songs here wouldn't have made his final cut, and other unrecorded gems we will never hear would have made it in.  But with that said, there is limited songwriting range here.  You will not find anything here like the experimental jazz of "Rainy Day, Dream Away", the manically inspired blues of "Voodoo Child (Slight Return)", the gorgeous melody, poetry and sensitivity of "The Wind Cries Mary" or the visionary musical journey of "1983".  These were all songs that revealed Jimi as the unpredictable and flamboyantly creative genius he was.  "First Rays" includes no such revelations, is more formulaic, and even includes a few tracks that you really don't need to hear more than once.  But a great album? Absolutely! And essential to your Hendrix collection.

reviewText: After the success of What's Going On, Marvin Gaye moved away from social issues to issues of the flesh. Let's Get It On finds him singing about sex, not just about the physical pleasure one gets, but on a spiritual level. The title track is almost sermon like in it's delivery where Mr. Gaye dispenses with all pleasantries and asks his lover to get it on. He not only feels good, but he feels sanctified. The song has a silky sound that matches Mr. Gaye's smooth vocals. The rest of the album finds Mr. Gaye searching for a love that will help him find that balance between the real and spiritual ecstasy he so desperately craves.

reviewText: Simon and Garfunkel were not just singers - they were incredibly talented poets who wrote words which touched your heart. Think of Shakespeare or Robert Frost put to music. You get not only the power of the words, but also the beauty fo the music.With Sounds of Silence, you get numerous classics - The Sounds of Silence, I Am a Rock, Kathy's Song for three. You also get a collection of less well known but just as intricate tunes - Leaves that are Green, Blessed, Somewhere they Can't Find Me, Anji, Richard Cory, A Most Peculiar Man, April Come She Will, We've got a Groovey Thing Goin'.Each song here has its own meaningful message. In I Am A Rock, they sing "I won't disturb the slumber of feelings that have died. If I never loved, I never would have cried." Quite a different view from 'Tis better to have loved and lost'!In The Sounds of Silence, they rail against people complacently accepting what they are told. "The people bowed and prayed to the neon god they made." Written back in 1965, the words are just as meaningful in modern times.Well recommended!

reviewText: I've said it about Bon Jovi and I'll say it about Billy Joel; the "typical" fan irritates me because they like the music for the weakest reasons.  A good beat, nostalgic and/or politically targeted lyrics, and pop mediocrity in general helped just about every album of Billy's aside from The Bridge into excessive-selling "classics" with some great songs and some adequate ones.  This album is not a majority fan-favorite.But "The Bridge" is good.  Consistently good, actually.  A common criticism is that it is a victim of 80's formula and production, but I only somewhat agree with that.  Indeed, without naming names, suffice to say that there are MANY other 80's albums that were far less full of artistic integrity.The album kicks off with a great piano statement, if underdeveloped.  The Piano Man indeed had not betrayed his roots for the synths-of-the-day, rather, he combined them with THE PIANO, which was vital for him, the music industry at the time, and myself, all for various reasons.  I often talk about the union of heart and brains, which for me is what really makes a good album.  I find "This is the Time," "A Matter of Trust," and "Temptation", beyond catchy. They are highly emotional, but they also connect with the emotions in a familiar-yet-unique sort of way, if that makes sense.  Billy's always had the rare talent of making simplicity endure the test of time, but i find the songs on this album FAR more MUSICALLY interesting than the dragging, monotone strums of "Captain Jack" and "Only the Good Die Young" and "Tell Her About It".Now that I have probably made a few million enemies, I should probably get to the nucleus of "The Bridge."  "Baby Grand" is one of those songs that comes along that you have to react with a "This is perfect." The presence of Ray Charles put it beyond perfect, but the song itself is just amazing.  The chords are a little more complex than Billy's usual recipe, the lyrics are very touching, and the SOUL and FEEL are so deep that you can play this quite a lot before being tired of it.  Everything about this song, from Billy and Ray, right down to each piano lick, is as tasteful as tasteful can get, and this is one of those songs that is the reason that music exists in the first place.There's another duet, "Code of Silence", with Cyndi Lauper,  which is pulsing and sensitive all at once, and another all-around great song.  "Big Man on Mulberry Street" is also a bit complex in the horn orchestration, and just like all the others here, a bit unique.  "Getting Closer" is a great way to end things, on a very positive thematic note.The only song that screams "too 80's" is "Modern Woman", with a poor choice in synth timbres, and for me a song with unnecessary subject matter.  Listening to that song and then some of the others in a certain order may taint the ears with a general residual impression of "80's", but 1) at worst it's still not that much and 2) that in itself isn't the worst thing in the world.None of Billy Joel's recordings will ever be considered a "desert island disc" for me, his albums are just too short and simple, and I think for more than a few of his fans, there's a nostalgic bug (which there's nothing wrong with).  But "The Bridge" is one of his more interesting and emotional albums, and its 40 minutes has very little filler.  To just start getting into Billy (which doesn't seem possible), don't get this first, but don't wait too long to get it, either.  Again, don't let others (including me) make your opinions for you.  His career is filled with great music all over the place.

reviewText: UK Soulstress Joss Stone returns on her third CD with a collection of songs she regards as more personal, as she was more creatively involved than on her previous two releases."Introducing Joss Stone" continues the retro soul vibe, but with more contemporary hip hop beats and scratches, and sleek production from neo soulster Raphael Saadiq.The bouncy, sassy, horn sprinkled "Headturner" is a great example of this. Lead off single "Tell me `bout it" sounds like something Aretha would do, complete with call and response backing vocals.  Similar is "Put your hands on me", driven by an insistent beat, matched with equally aggressive vocals.The more mellow and soothing "Tell me what we gonna do now" features a breezy rap by Common and nice acoustic guitar.Standouts to me are "Music", and ode to her passion music, with a rap from Lauryn Hill, (sounding very much like something off Lauryn's classic "Miseducation of Lauryn Hill" cd), sparse but catchy bassline, and sprinkled with guitar and horns. Brilliant!"Arms of my baby" is another delightful number with tempo shifts from smooth R&B; in the verses to an almost salsa feel in the chorus. The harmonies are stunning too.Completing the trio of excellence is the sleek, choppy retro funk of "Bad habit", which sounds very much like something Raphael Saadiq's former band, Lucy Pearl would do.The charming, hook laden "Baby baby baby" sounds very Motown, Jackson 5 to be exact, while "What were we thinking" is a seventies sounding ballad with a soothing wall of harmonies, cutting strings and a stirring vocal delivery from Joss.Ladies and gentlemen, introducing all over again, Joss Stone!!

reviewText: "When your backs against the wall, you gotta bang your way out" (Lil Kim "Gon Delirious 2002). I'm willing to bet that this was the motivation that Ja Rule had in his head during the entire recording process of R.U.L.E. See Ja had become one of the leading rap stars in the game, with multi-platinum album after multi-platinum album and top ten single after top ten single. He was riding high an undeniable wave of success, and it seemed that his fire would never diminish. However his beef with another rapper, 50 Cent is what really hurt his carrer. 50 was the big dog on campus for a few months and ripped into Ja, much to the fans delight. However now that 50 has completely fallen off the face of the earth, its time for Ja to come out swinging.The album's first single "Wonderful" featuring R. Kelly & Ashanti is one of Rule's finest moments. A remix to "I Wonder" (which is no where to be found), the track is pop enough to dominate radio but street enough where Ja doesn't have to be dressed in a Grease varsity jacket a la "Mesmerized". And I never thought I would say this, but the inclusion of Ashanti was a wise decision. And with "New York, New York" featuring Fat Joe & Jadakiss starting to turn up on radio, its safe to say that he is going to have the urban radio market in the palm of his hand for quite some time.And while there are good things going on here, the album is still weak being that Ja doesn't register as much of a rapper. Lyrically he will not considered for the greatest of all time. Comments like "the streets damn near raised me" in "The INC" intro are what had Ja on the chopping block in the first place; he is much to soft to be claiming to be a gangsta. "Last of the Mohicans" has an infectious beat, but Ja fails to ride the beat, and the hook provided by Black Child just doesn't fit the record.It's tracks like "Get it Started" featuring the angelic voice of City High's Claudette Ortiz is where Ja feels most comfortable, and he sounds his best. So while he may not be the toughest dude in the game, thats ok he can bring it as the second coming of LL. It was that formula that made him all his cash anyway. Guest appearences by Llyod & Trick Daddy are worth a mention as well. I don't think Ja will have a hard time regaining the respect of his core audience, but its the street audience that is going to be his toughest challenge, and R.U.L.E. isn't going to be his homecoming welcome that he dreamed of. And my final thought, where is Charli Baltimore?

reviewText: Sarah McLachlan did it again, without really doing something.This record contained all the tracks she recorded for soundtracks, other artists' records or performed during special live performances since the first Rarities, B-Sides and Other Stuff (1996).It's gotta be said that this is a great album with many highlights. Especially when you consider that most artists don't even release rarities records at all.It starts out with 'Ordinary Miracle' from the movie Charlotte's Web. And this is not the only soundtrack recording represented on this compilation. Sarah's version of The Beatles' 'Blackbird' from I am Sam is beautiful and stays very true to the original and 'When She Loved Me' (Toy Story 2) is very touching. The absolute highight of this cd for me is 'The Rainbow Connection' (from The Muppets), this song goes straight to the bottom of my heart everytime I listen to it.There are also some very interesting duets on this album. 'Just Like Me' with DMC or 'Time after Time' with Cyndi Lauper are very nice additions to Sarah's catalogue. 'Angel' (live) with the amazing Emmmylou Harris and 'Pills' met The perishers are simply wonderful. But the outstanding duet has got to be 'Don't Let Go' with Bryan Adams (from the animation movie Spirit: Stallion of the Cimarron).'Prayer of St. Francis' and 'Unchained Melody' (in a totally onrecognizable version!) are two very interesting recordings and show how many different sides and styles there are to miss McLachlan.And just like on Rarities, B-Sides and Other Stuff volume 1, there's another Joni Mitchell cover on this volume; 'River'.Yes she recorded River for her 2006 season album Wintersong, but the nice thing is that this version is a different one.I'm a big Joni Mitchell fan myself and don't really like it when people cover her songs, but Sarah's versions of Blue and River make me wish she will one day release a record full of Joni Mitchell covers.One can always dream, right?And dream is something this cd will surely let you do. The voice, the words, the music... Sarah goes straight into the heart of her listeners.If you don't already have this cd, get it now. You won't regret it!
summary: A great gift to the fans

But the outstanding duet has got to be 'Don't Let Go' with Bryan Adams (from the animation movie Spirit: Stallion of the Cimarron).'Prayer of St. Francis' and 'Unchained Melody' (in a totally onrecognizable version!) are two very interesting recordings and show how many different sides and styles there are to miss McLachlan.And just like on Rarities, B-Sides and Other Stuff volume 1, there's another Joni Mitchell cover on this volume; 'River'.Yes she recorded River for her 2006 season album Wintersong, but the nice thing is that this version is a different one.I'm a big Joni Mitchell fan myself and don't really like it when people cover her songs, but Sarah's versions of Blue and River make me wish she will one day release a record full of Joni Mitchell covers.One can always dream, right?And dream is something this cd will surely let you do. The voice, the words, the music... Sarah goes straight into the heart of her listeners.If you don't already have this cd, get it now. You won't regret it!

reviewText: I'll admit that I was one of Natalie's detractors when "Torn" was played into the ground a few years ago. I was about to write her off as a one-hit wonder but that all changed when I heard the first single off her new album "White Lilies Island", called "Wrong Impression". The song itself is even catchier than "Torn", a song I once loved but grew tired of. When I heard the entire album I was definitely a changed person. This album has definitely altered my perception and attitude towards Natalie. I absolutely adore this album. Every song on this album just impressed me so much that I have completely forgiven Natalie for "Torn". "Everything Goes" is a perhaps my favorite ballad on this album. It's quiet, subdued, and emotional. The opening riffs to "Hurricane" definitely has some Garbage influences in the first few seconds, as does the following track "Sunlight". Apparently Natalie has been listening to a lot of Garbage and maybe Joydrop with that same electronic/rock vibe."That Day" and "Beauty on Fire" is an excellent way to open up the album. There were even moments when Natalie's vocals sounded a bit like Ani Difranco. "Goodbye" is a stunning ballad that is just as good as "Everything Goes". None of the tracks on this album sounds anything like "Torn" which is a good thing. My only flaw with this album is that I can't play it on my computer at work which really annoys me to no ends of the earth (thank you very much RCA Records). Nevertheless I love this album. I'm not going to give it up just because I can't listen to it on my computer at work.

reviewText: It's hard for me to give anything but five stars for most of Luther's Cds as they are really good and his voice is really a wonder. I'd have to say he is one of my favourites and for years I said `my favourite living singer' but now he also has transitioned -joining the late Marvin Gaye, Ronnie Dyson, Donny Hathaway, Levi Stubbs, David Ruffin and others for me, May their souls all rest in peace.Luther came to Jamaica in 2001 and I had always said `there are some singers you like and you buy their cds  but you may not necessarily make the effort to go to their concert but if Luther comes to Jamaica you know I'll be there'. So said so done! When he came this album was to  be released the following week and he debuted the song `Can I take You Out?' and taught it to the audience. It was great..It was raining lightly but we just put up our umbrellas , no problem. We got the CD as it came out. This was his last CD of new material released before he passed. It is a good Listen and a worthy addition to the collection of any Luther fan. My favourites on this: I'd Rather, Can Heaven Wait, Any Day Now.

They've only gotten smarter, and even their slight slip-ups (Hail to the Thief) are more stunning than anything anyone else is doing.

reviewText: As Motown began its migration from Detroit to Los Angeles, Motown Productions had already experienced a wealth of critical and commercial success in television with the award winning, Neilsen #1 "T.C.B." and "G.I.T." television specials. That was followed up with a repeat success with Diana Ross' Emmy nominated, Neislen winning debut television special from 1971' "Diana!" and then The Jackson Five "Goin' Back to Indiana" with almost the identical cast to Diana. And then "The Temptations TV Show". They began moving into the movies in a big way with the Oscar nominated, "Lady Sings the Blues" starring the Queen of Motown, Diana Ross. Marvin Gaye had also starred in 2 movies,"Chrome and Hot Leather" and "The Ballad of Andy Crocker". Motown's involvement in those projects remains unclear. However, Motown did indeed release Marvin's soundtrack to the blaxipoiltation movie, "Trouble Man" joining his peers issac Hayes and Curtis Mayfield. Marvin garnered a Top 10 Hot 100 single with the bluesy/jazzy title track that also went Top 5 R&B taking the soundtrack to platinum level sales with a Top 15 Pop Album and to the upper reaches of the R&B Album chart (#3)! Marvin remained true to the soundtrack and score without trying to create a pop/R&B album with single candidates. The title track would be the only single released. Despite that, there were several programmable instrumentals that received a respectable amount of quiet storm and even jazz airplay on "Don't Mess with Mr. T", "Poor Abbey Walsh" and "Cleo's Apartment" for instance. Though Marvin had acting roles in the aforementioned movies, he would only be responsible for the soundtrack to "Trouble Man". After the phenomenal, still building success of "What's Going On", Marvin also released the Top 10 single, "You're the Man" continuing in the socio-political slant of "What's Going On". "Trouble Man" was a straight ahead look at live in the inner city ghettos. Time has only proven that Marvin had a natural understanding of jazz even beyond his love of vocal crooning. Now Motown has given "Trouble Man" the Expanded Edition treatment, something afforded The Supremes, Diana Ross, Smokey Robinson and Marvin Gaye catalog.

reviewText: The Flaming Lips are not a band easily placed in one simple category.  Their sound covers such a wide spectrum of musical styles.  Words that can describe them are quirky, catchy, psychedelic, bombastic, poppy, progressive, bizarre, talented, etc.  Catch my drift?  They are all over the place, but throw all of that into a pile, and the result you get is The Flaming Lips.  And this is all on display on "At War with the Mystics," which is probably my favorite album of theirs to date.  I know that is heresy to the many who have longed considered "The Soft Bulletin" their masterpiece, or to those who have nostalgic pinings for the band to return to their crazed, indie rock-driven days of the early to mid 90's, but nothing I have heard by the band sounds as collectively good as this record does.  Trying to describe each song would be an exercise in futility.  I know it is old hat to say that words do not do their music justice, but I swear, in the case of this band, that really is the truth!  Once you listen to this record, you will understand what I mean.

reviewText: Dolly Parton once said that "The hardest thing for a performer to demonstrate is sincerity. Once you can fake that, you've got it made." Eminem would like us to think he's highly sincere, with his unending self-gratification, but with this third (or fourth, if you count the labored D-12 disc) CD he begins to come across as self-aware. He's the hero of suburban kids everywhere he proclaims in "White America". He's a ticking time-bomb in "Soldier" and "My Dad's Gone Crazy". He's a dedicated father in "Hallie's Song". He's this, he's that, he's the other and then he's back again. At what point does all this superego hopscotch become valid and at what point does it become the Eminmen Copyrighted Selling Point, that he can summon at will, and will continue to do so for as long as it makes a buck? I ask this because even as you're bobbing your head to the relentless beats conjured by Em and Dre, you'll still be getting the sense of deja vu. It really is the Eminem Show with Em, Mom, Kim, Hallie, Dre, and the nutty cast of characters popping in and out. He's as vocally dexterous as ever, (we could spend all day reciting the witty and memorable lines displayed in just a few songs.) and as I stated, songs like "Square Dance" and of course "Without Me" are guaranteed car-radio hits.It's just this: even hit sitcoms run out of new ideas, and Em is well on his way there; after he gets through ragging on family members, he contrives enemies out of thin air, (MTV tried to shut him down? The Source doesn't respect him?) Worst of all, he's starting to indulge in vulgarity for vulgarity's sake like Too Short or 2 Live Crew with the ultra-misogynistic "Drip" and "Superman"; it's not just that these tracks are disgusting, it's that after staking his claim as the ultimate individual, such pandering like this should be beneath him. Those quibbles aside, it's another fun filled hour with MM, and he'll undoubtedly be renewed next season, even if the ratings start to shudder.

reviewText: After releasing four studio albums full of mostly accessible dance-pop/pop balladry, Madonna seemed to have decided to go for something a little different.  Always one to be at the forefront of pop culture, EROTICA was Madonna's record geared toward the underground rave/dance culture.  Continuing the thread begun with 'Justify My Love', EROTICA features hard, cold dance beats coupled with Madonna's most detached vocal work to date.  Because it was such a distinct departure from her previous work, the album was met initially with mediocre response, despite its' attempt to be "erotic".  I personally hated it the first time I listened to it.  No, this is probably the first(and only)Madonna record that takes repeated listens in order to ingratiate itself  into the brain.  None of the tracks jump out upon first listen with the exception of the very fine 'Rain', still one of Madonna's best ballads.  The title track is essentially a 'Justify My Love' rehash with a different producer.  The album had several potential hits, but for some reason such snoozers as  the appropriately titled 'Bad Girl' and the house rave-up wannabe and just plain bad 'Deeper and Deeper'were the tracks selected to essentially represent the album.  Besides the aforementioned 'Rain',  other standouts include 'Thief of Hearts' and 'Waiting'.  For those who didn't give this record a  second listen, give it another try.  Now that Madonna is reinventing her sound with literally every album, just think of this as the beginning of something great.

Grace and company give me faith that rock isn't dead. The music is easy to listen to but very dynamic. It will appeal to a passive listener as well as a musician. The album flows perfectly. I'm definitely a fan now. This album is packed with energy, softness, emotion, and so many other things. I hope you enjoy it as much as I have.

reviewText: In the first few moments of Porcupine Tree's major label debut, I found myself afraid that the band had forsaken its traditional sound for something else.  But "Blackest Eyes" quickly settled into more familiar territory.  The rest of In Absentia followed.Similar to previous efforts, Stupid Dream and Lightbulb Sun, In Absentia showcases the songwriting ability and musical talents of Steve Wilson and crew.  The music is atmospheric with soaring guitars, excellent bass and keyboard work, and huge drums.  As usual, vocal harmonies are plentiful.There is a slightly harder edge to some of the songs and a greater sense of whimsy in a few instances but these elements add to, not distract from, the overall focus of the album.  All-in-all, this is another great album from Porcupine Tree.

reviewText: As you've probably read in the other reviews, this was the first album on their new label, and the first album with new guitarist, Sonny Mayo. I was worried about them losing Clint Lowery, because he had a great guitar sound and wrote some great riffs. While Mayo is most definitely NOT Lowery, he nonetheless delivers some exceptional guitar playing, and you almost don't notice the change. Almost. The main difference I see between this cd and previous ones, is that it lacks the instrumental hooks that were abundant on their other releases. That's not to say they aren't there, but they just aren't as obvious to the listener. It almost seems awkward at times, like they are still trying to gel with Mayo after playing with Lowery for so long. Lajon's vocals are top-notch as always, and the cd is worth buying for that reason alone.Despite some short-comings in the hook department, there is not a bad song on the album. It is a solid listen from front to back, and you probably won't be skipping any songs. The singles "Ugly" and "Pieces" are probably the two best songs on here. The main thing you'll notice, I think, is that these songs won't stick in your head like previous favorites, such as: "Denial", "Praise", "Bitch" and "Enemy". However, this is still light years better than most music being released on the heavy music scene. Even though this is my least favorite 7Dust album, it still gets a 4/5 from me.
summary: 5th release takes a step back to their earlier days.

reviewText: Robert Mile's DREAMLAND is probably my favorite trance album to date. It's dreamy soundscape has a much softer tone to it than most other artists in this genre which makes for a nice release from all the happy dance music flooding mainstream radio today. Don't misconstrue what I'm saying, though. Dirty Vegas, Kylie Minogue and Paulina Rubio are among the best artists to emerge in 2002 but I've recently needed a break from all these sappy love songs and wannabe dance anthems, so I turned (with little surprise) to the old but never out-dated DREAMLAND by Robert Miles. 23 AM (which is a little more new-agey than this) is another amazing album by Robert Miles but I think that DREAMLAND still remains my favorite. I might buy ORGANIK someday but from what I've heard it's not too great, which is hard for me to fathom because everything I've ever heard from Robert Miles is simply amazing... DREAMLAND is a fine mixture of smooth electronica, new age and trance.My favorite songs include "In My Dreams", "Children (Dream Version)", "Fable (Messsage Version)", and "One And One", which both feature the gorgeous vocals of Maria Nayler who deeply contributes to the album's magical and very surreal atmosphere which is sheer heaven to the senses. So do the world a favor by purchasing this masterpiece of an album which is probably already considered a classic to trance fans that know a gem when they hear it.This is highly recommended.

reviewText: There is no doubt about this year in the way of albums that are out. most of them have felt like you've wasted your money on something that felt like garbage. It has been very sad. Nevertheless, there are some artists that have really known how to make a great album time and time again. That absolutely has been the case with Vanessa Williams. It has been 4 years since her last album, 2005's Everlasting Love, and she has proven that she has more life in her music and acting than ever. With the massive success of her work on Ugly Betty, Vanessa has been introduced boldly to a whole new generation of fans. Now she is back to sing her soulful little heart out again, and this time it definitely is a winner.Vanessa Williams 2009 album The Real Thing is definitely a well-rendered and delightful return to form for Vanessa's sultry voice. The album contains a nice and simple mix of quiet storm, R&B;, Jazz and Latin rhythms. The songs here really work very well for Vanessa, and shows how much she has delivered well. The album includes a lot of great tracks including the sultry and seductive Breathless, the Jazz Standard Lazy Afternoon, as well as other great songs like the title track The Real thing, and the easy and mellow Hello Like Before. Sadly though there are a few disadvantages with the album. The first is that it is very short, and leaves hard core listeners going wild for more. The second disadvantage is that I was hoping for a bit more variety in the songs, considering there could've been a few more upbeat songs to the mix. Still, Vanessa carries through on the album very well, by letting her simple and soulful voice carry through the album beautifully.While there really haven't been very many albums that have worked this past year, Vanessa Williams still knows how to make a album work well. If you haven't yet heard a Vanessa Williams song, or if you are a hard core fan of Ugly Betty, than this would be a great download for your MP3 Player.  So than you'll finally hear why Vanessa Williams is still The Real Thing for over 20 years as a singer.Songs: B+Price: BMastering: BOverall: B+

reviewText: This album is Carly's follow up to her very successful "Coming Around Again" album (although technically, "My Romance" was released before this album).  While it didn't quite reach the commercial success of the previous album, in many ways it is a better album.  Her writing, vocals and performances are top notch.  She lets her sense of humor ("Don't Wrap It Up") and playfulness ("Holding Me Tonight") come through in her lyrics.  She performs one song with her sister Lucy Simon and Judy Collins.  But perhaps my favorite song is the last track ("We Just Got Here") which is one of the most honest songs about middle age I've ever heard.  This album holds up much better musically over time because the arrangements are a lot more acoustic than the previous album and Carly musicianship shines through.

reviewText: This album was a tremendous accomplishment.  A gem of all gems, the mother load of everything rebellious.  Everything was congruous for the band; rage came from living in LA. Every song is a masterpiece in its own right, a statement of how growing up in LA can affect someone.This band's energy and intelligence were so compelling, so in depth, so genuine.Freedom was their first ever video.  I remember reading an interview where Zack was saying how they (The whole band) was hanging out on his parents couch, and the video came on for the first time.  I remember the video well.  I doubt MTV will ever play it again.  I had to see it on the Headbanger's Ball.  It aired maybe twice on the Headbanger's Ball, and then was never to be seen again.  Too "serious" for the MTV community. "...Brother, did you forget your name, did you lose it on the wall.... listen closely to the end of this verse, Zack whispers something very important here (See title of review).  I think he forgot his own message only moments after uttering the words.Take the Power Back is a brilliant song, featured in such movies as Natural Born Killers, look for the scene where Woody busts out of jail.Bombtrack is also a great song, featured in Matrix, at the very end of the movie.Fistful of Steel is their greatest song in my opinion, both lyrically speaking and musically, this song was an inspiration to me for years in the early 90's.  "Not a silent one, but a defiant one, never a normal one, 'cause Im ......."Brilliance, on a record.  That's about it.  If you haven't purchased this album, you're completely missing out on a terrific jolt to the music community.Unfortunately, Rage never grew or improved, and instead milked their wonderful sound until there was nothing left, not even Rage.  In my opinion, this is their only accomplishment.
